rows.title: Business Combinations: the Acquisition Method, Goodwill and Common Control
rows.snippet: The theory of accounting for an acquisition from the definition of a business to pooling of interests, worked from Barito Pacific's 2025 purchases and set beside the industries where the boundary matters most
rows.author: Dika Gustiana
rows.content:
In brief

  • A business combination is a transaction in which an acquirer obtains control of a business. Buying a set of assets that is not a business is an asset acquisition: the price is spread over the assets on relative fair values, and no goodwill or bargain purchase gain arises. The optional concentration test settles many cases quickly.

  • Under the acquisition method (PSAK 103) the acquirer measures the consideration and every identifiable asset and liability at acquisition-date fair value, including intangibles the seller never recorded. Goodwill is the residual. A negative residual is a bargain purchase gain in profit or loss, recognised only after the numbers have been rechecked. Provisional amounts may be corrected for up to one year.

  • When the same party controls both sides, nothing is bought from an outsider, so PSAK 338 replaces fair values with carrying amounts (pooling of interests) and puts the difference from the price in additional paid-in capital.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) report a gain from bargain purchase of 1,868,039 for 2025, in USD thousand, against profit for the year of 1,615,634 (BRPT FS 2025, statement of profit or loss, PDF p. 17). Two purchases by its petrochemical subsidiary produced it.

After reading this page a student should be able to classify a purchase, apply the acquisition method, allocate the excess of price over book value, handle the measurement period and record a common-control combination.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. Why companies combine and the legal forms

The legal form of a combination decides whose ledger the acquired assets land in, not how they are measured. The lecture notes (AKL Chapter 1) list the motives, from cost savings to tax, and classify combinations as horizontal (same line of business), vertical and conglomerate (unrelated lines). Vertical integration joins different stages of one supply chain, a refinery buying its crude supplier, rather than firms in "pasar yang berbeda" (different markets), as the notes put it.

Measurement is the same for all three. In a merger the values go into A's ledger; in a stock acquisition they appear only on the consolidation worksheet (section 7). BRPT's 2025 purchases were stock acquisitions. CAPGC Pte. Ltd., a subsidiary of PT Chandra Asri Pacific Tbk (CAP), bought 100 percent of the shares of Aster Chemical and Energy Pte. Ltd. (ACE) from Shell Singapore (Note 1d, PDF p. 43).

2. What is a business: combination or asset acquisition

The acquisition method applies only when what is acquired is a business. PSAK 103 Kombinasi Bisnis (formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3) scopes out the acquisition of an asset or group of assets that is not a business (para. 2(b)) and combinations of entities under common control (para. 2(c)). The notes never define a business.

A business needs an input and a substantive process. A business is an integrated set of activities and assets capable of being managed to provide goods or services to customers. Outputs are not required, but it needs at least an input and a substantive process that together significantly contribute to the ability to create outputs (para. B8). An operating wind farm with turbines, a power purchase agreement (PPA) and staff is a business; a development licence with no workforce is usually not.

The concentration test is a shortcut out of the definition. Since 1 January 2021 an optional test, elected deal by deal (paras. B7A–B7B), applies. If substantially all of the fair value of the gross assets acquired is concentrated in a single identifiable asset or a group of similar assets, the set is not a business and no further analysis is needed. Cash, deferred tax assets and goodwill from deferred tax are left out of gross assets, and a tangible asset and an intangible asset are never "similar".

For example (illustration), take BRPT's acquisition of 51 percent of PT Lombok Timur Bayu Energi, a wind project company, on 3 January 2024 (Note 43, PDF pp. 231–232).

Gross assets acquired = 1 cash + 44 receivables + 2 other current + 37 fixed assets + 7,700 project development costs = 7,784

Gross assets excluding cash = 7,783

Concentration = 7,700 / 7,783 = 98.9%, substantially all in one asset

The boundary changes five things. Suppose (illustration) the buyer also paid 150 of legal fees and, had the project been a business, the development rights would have been valued independently at 6,078.

3. The acquisition method: acquirer and acquisition date

Control, not legal form or the signing date, fixes both the acquirer and the acquisition date, the first two of the method's four steps (para. 5).

The acquirer is the entity that obtains control under PSAK 110 Laporan Keuangan Konsolidasian (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) (para. B13). When that is unclear, the standard looks at who pays, who issues shares, whose owners and managers dominate afterwards, and relative size (paras. B14–B17). In a reverse acquisition, typical of a backdoor listing, the owners of a private company receive enough new shares of a listed shell to control it, so the private company is the accounting acquirer (para. B19).

The acquisition date is the date control passes, usually the closing date, which may differ from the signing date (paras. 8–9). It fixes the fair values, the start of consolidation and the measurement period. Shell announced its agreement to sell to CAPGC on 8 May 2024, but control passed at completion on 1 April 2025, the acquisition date in Note 43 (PDF p. 226). Aster Polymer Solutions Pte. Ltd. (APS) follows the same pattern: agreement on 6 May 2025, effective and consolidated from 1 August 2025 (PDF pp. 228–229).

4. Consideration transferred and acquisition-related costs

Consideration, the price the acquirer pays, is measured at fair value: cash paid, other assets given up, liabilities incurred to the former owners, and equity issued (para. 37). The notes' Pop Corporation example issues 100,000 shares of USD 10 par, market price USD 16, for the net assets of Son.

Consideration = 100,000 × 16 = 1,600,000; common stock = 100,000 × 10 = 1,000,000; paid-in capital = 600,000

Dr Investment in Son 1,600,000 / Cr Common stock 1,000,000; Cr Paid-in capital 600,000

Acquisition-related costs are not part of the price. Advisory, legal, accounting, valuation and internal acquisition-department costs are expensed when incurred, and the costs of issuing debt or equity follow PSAK 232 and PSAK 109 (para. 53). The notes' example reaches the same result: the 80,000 consultant fee is expensed, and SEC fees, accountants' fees and share certificates (5,000 + 10,000 + 25,000 = 40,000) reduce paid-in capital.

Dr Investment expense 80,000; Dr Paid-in capital 40,000 / Cr Cash 120,000

Deferred consideration, a fixed amount payable later, is part of the consideration at fair value and a liability from the acquisition date. ACE's provisional consideration of 671,970 was 388,745 in cash at completion plus 283,225 deferred (Note 43, PDF p. 227).

Contingent consideration depends on a future event, such as an earn-out. It enters the consideration at acquisition-date fair value (para. 39) and is classified as a liability or equity under PSAK 232 (para. 40). Later a liability is remeasured through profit or loss and an equity amount is not remeasured; neither touches goodwill after the measurement period (para. 58, restated in BRPT's policy, Note 3d, PDF p. 69). For example (illustration), an earn-out of 10,000 on two years' wind output is worth 2,800 at acquisition and 4,000 a year later.

At acquisition: included in consideration, Cr Contingent consideration liability 2,800

One year later: Dr Loss on remeasurement of contingent consideration 1,200 / Cr Contingent consideration liability 1,200

5. Recognising and measuring what was acquired

The acquirer recognises the identifiable assets and liabilities separately from goodwill (para. 10), at acquisition-date fair value (para. 18). Each must meet the definition of an asset or liability at that date, so a restructuring the buyer merely plans is not a liability (para. 11), and each must be part of the exchange, not a separate deal with the seller (para. 12).

Items the seller never recorded are still recognised. An internally built brand, a customer list or a favourable contract is invisible in the seller's books but identifiable to a buyer (para. 13; see the Intangible Assets essay). A contingent liability is recognised if it is a present obligation whose fair value can be measured, even if an outflow is not probable, which PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37) would not allow outside a combination (para. 23).

Deferred tax and employee benefits follow their own standards. BRPT's policy names deferred tax under PSAK 212 (formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12) and employee benefits under PSAK 219 (formerly PSAK 24, IAS 19) (Note 3d, PDF p. 68).

In the notes' Pam–Sun example Sun's book net assets of 750,000 become 1,200,000 at fair value, including an unrecorded patent of 50,000 and notes payable revalued down to 135,000. Their allocation entry debits "Building – net $850.000", which is building 500,000 plus equipment 350,000. It balances, but equipment needs its own line because the two have different lives.

6. Goodwill and bargain purchase

Goodwill is what the consideration buys beyond the identifiable net assets: synergies, the assembled workforce, expected new customers. It cannot be sold on its own, so it is measured as a residual (para. 32).

Goodwill = consideration transferred + NCI + fair value of any previously held interest − identifiable net assets at fair value

The notes' two Pam–Sun cases, with identifiable net assets of 1,200,000:

Case 1: goodwill

Case 2: bargain purchase

Consideration

400,000 cash + 50,000 shares × 20 = 1,400,000

40,000 shares × 20 + 200,000 bonds = 1,000,000

Residual

1,400,000 − 1,200,000 = 200,000 goodwill

1,000,000 − 1,200,000 = 200,000 gain

A bargain purchase must survive a recheck. A negative residual often signals an error. Before recognising a gain the acquirer must reassess whether it has identified every asset and liability and review how it measured the net assets, any NCI, any previously held interest and the consideration (para. 36). Whatever remains is a gain in profit or loss on the acquisition date, attributed to the acquirer (para. 34). Forced sales and sellers leaving a business are the usual causes (para. 35). The notes go straight to the gain; their Case 2 also assumes the 10 percent bonds are worth their face value of 200,000, which holds only if 10 percent is the market rate.

Take ACE as the starting point (Note 43, PDF p. 227): identifiable net assets at fair value, after deferred tax, of 2,444,134 against a provisional consideration of 671,970.

Gain = 2,444,134 − 671,970 = 1,772,164

Dr Cash 215,431; Dr Receivables 680,565; Dr Inventories 970,281; Dr Other current assets 6; Dr Right-of-use assets 307,351; Dr Fixed assets 1,604,141 / Cr Trade and other payables 563,778; Cr Other current liabilities 23,502; Cr Decommissioning and other provisions 121,519; Cr Lease liabilities 377,366; Cr Deferred tax liabilities 247,476; Cr Cash 388,745; Cr Deferred consideration 283,225; Cr Gain from bargain purchase 1,772,164

BRPT attributes the gain to a different view of ACE's strategic direction between the seller and the group. For example (illustration), had the para. 36 review found an environmental obligation with a fair value of 50,000 that the valuation missed, the gain would fall by 50,000 before deferred tax, to 1,722,164.

7. Purchase price allocation: from book value to goodwill

On a stock acquisition the parent's ledger shows only the investment, so the fair values are rebuilt on the worksheet. The notes for AKL Chapter 3 use an allocation schedule: price minus the subsidiary's book equity is the excess, which goes first to identifiable items whose fair value differs from book value, the remainder to goodwill.

Take as the starting point BRPT's acquisition of PT UPC Sidrap Bayu Energi (SBE), operator of a 75 MW wind farm with a 30-year PPA with PLN, the state electricity company, on 2 April 2024 (Note 43, PDF pp. 233–234). BRPT reports identifiable net assets of 38,459 before the PPA, a customer contract (the PPA) of 78,709, deferred tax liabilities on the step-ups of 20,941, goodwill of 12,051 and consideration of 108,278. Ownership of 99.99 percent is treated here as 100 percent. BRPT does not give SBE's book equity; assume 31,000 for illustration.

Excess of price over book equity = 108,278 − 31,000 = 77,278

Dr SBE share capital and retained earnings 31,000; Dr Fixed assets and other items 7,459; Dr Customer contract 78,709; Dr Goodwill 12,051 / Cr Deferred tax liability 20,941; Cr Investment in SBE 108,278

Debits and credits are both 129,219; K2 amortises the PPA afterwards.

Deferred tax can turn a gain into goodwill. Buying shares does not change the subsidiary's tax bases, so every fair value step-up is a taxable temporary difference (carrying amount above tax base, taxed as the asset is used), and PSAK 212 requires the deferred tax liability to be recognised in the acquisition accounting, which raises goodwill by the same amount (PSAK 103 para. 24 sends deferred tax to PSAK 212). For example (illustration), a step-up of 10,000 on turbines at a 22 percent tax rate:

Deferred tax liability = 22% × 10,000 = 2,200; goodwill rises by 2,200

Each year the 1,000 of extra depreciation (ten-year life) releases 22% × 1,000 = 220: Dr Deferred tax liability 220 / Cr Deferred tax expense 220

No deferred tax is recognised on goodwill itself (PSAK 212 para. 15(a)), because goodwill is the residual and a liability on it would raise goodwill again. At SBE, BREN's tax note puts 17,316 = 22% × 78,709 of the 20,941 on the contract and the rest on other step-ups (BREN FS 2025, PDF p. 121). Without the deferred tax line, identifiable net assets would be 38,459 + 78,709 = 117,168, above the price.

117,168 − 108,278 = 8,890 bargain purchase gain, instead of goodwill of 12,051

The notes' schedules leave deferred tax out.

With less than 100 percent, NCI enters the residual. In the notes' Pam–Son case (90 percent for 10,200,000; identifiable net assets at fair value 7,000,000) the price is grossed up to an "Implied fair value of sun ($10.200.000÷90%)" of 11,333,333, so NCI is 1,133,333 and goodwill 4,333,333. PSAK 103 para. 19 allows NCI at fair value, but measured on the minority shares themselves, which carry no control premium, or at the proportionate share; the NCI essay works through the choice.

Proportionate: NCI = 10% × 7,000,000 = 700,000; goodwill = 10,200,000 + 700,000 − 7,000,000 = 3,900,000

The notes' allocation entry also omits Dr Goodwill 4,333,333; as printed it debits 1,400,000 and credits 5,733,333.

8. The measurement period

Provisional amounts can be corrected against goodwill for up to one year, because valuing a refinery or a long-term contract takes months. Provisional amounts are adjusted retrospectively for new information about facts that existed at the acquisition date (para. 45). Adjustments go against goodwill or the bargain purchase gain (para. 48), and comparatives are revised as if the final figures had been booked at the acquisition date (para. 49). After the year, only errors are corrected (para. 50).

For example (illustration), BRPT paid 101,927 at completion, and a later verification required another 6,351 (Note 43, PDF p. 233). Suppose the 6,351 had been agreed eight months after closing, from completion accounts as at the acquisition date.

Initial goodwill = 101,927 − (38,459 + 78,709 − 20,941) = 101,927 − 96,227 = 5,700

Adjustment within the measurement period: Dr Goodwill 6,351 / Cr Payable to sellers 6,351; final goodwill = 12,051

BRPT's 2025 figures have two provisional elements. ACE's consideration "is provisional as the final consideration is subject to arbitration proceedings" (Note 43, PDF p. 227). APS's fair values and its gain of 95,875 are labelled provisional, and its purchase price allocation report is dated 23 March 2026 (PDF pp. 228–229).

9. Push-down accounting

Push-down accounting, which ends the notes' Chapter 3, has no PSAK counterpart. In it the subsidiary rewrites its own books to the parent's price, revaluing assets, recording goodwill and replacing retained earnings with "push-down capital". In their example Pop pays 5,000 shares at USD 55 plus 100,000 cash for Son.

Price = 5,000 × 55 + 100,000 = 375,000; Son's identifiable net assets at fair value = 590,000 − 250,000 = 340,000; goodwill = 35,000

Their balance sheet for Son prints "Goodwill $70.000" against total assets of 625,000, which fit 35,000; 70,000 is Son's land.

Under PSAK a subsidiary's own statements stay on its carrying amounts (the figures already in its books), because goodwill recorded there would be internally generated, which PSAK 238 forbids. PSAK 338's basis for conclusions uses the term differently, for carrying a parent's earlier purchase price allocation into a later common-control transfer. The 2012 text calls that conceptually right (DK19) but rules it out for common-control combinations as impracticable (DK22), and the 2025 revision moves towards it (section 10). The fair values therefore live only on the worksheet, with the same numbers:

Dr Capital stock 150,000; Dr Retained earnings 110,000; Dr Inventories 20,000; Dr Land 40,000; Dr Equipment 40,000; Dr Goodwill 35,000 / Cr Building 20,000; Cr Investment in Son 375,000

10. Business combinations under common control

When one party controls both sides before and after a transfer, no outsider has set the consideration, so fair values lose their anchor. PSAK 103 excludes these transfers (para. 2(c)), and Indonesia applies PSAK 338 Kombinasi Bisnis Entitas Sepengendali (formerly PSAK 38), set out with an acquisition-versus-pooling table in the Share Capital essay. The receiving entity pools: carrying amounts, no goodwill, the difference from the consideration in additional paid-in capital (APIC), never recycled, and comparatives restated (Note 3e, PDF pp. 70–71).

Buying out a minority holder shows where the boundary sits. PSAK 338 para. 09 reads: "Transaksi pembelian saham atau aset neto milik pemegang saham nonpengendali (yang tidak berada dalam pengendalian yang sama dengan pemegang saham pengendali) merupakan transaksi yang mencakup perubahan substansi ekonomi kepemilikan dari pemegang saham nonpengendali ke pemegang saham pengendali. Oleh karena itu, transaksi ini bukan merupakan transaksi kombinasi bisnis entitas sepengendali." Only a minority holder outside the common control is excluded.

For example (illustration, sized on BRPT's 2025 purchase in section 12), a group company pays 200,000 for 51 percent minority stakes in two companies it already controls. The stakes are carried in the consolidated statements as NCI of 161,296.

Neither route touches profit; only the equity line differs. Had the group not controlled the companies before, PSAK 103 would apply instead, with fair values and goodwill.

Carrying amounts carry old acquisitions with them. Goodwill that a transferred business recognised on an earlier third-party purchase moves across at its carrying amount (section 12 traces one case at BRPT). The 2025 revision of PSAK 338, effective 1 January 2026, switches to the transferring entity's carrying amounts rather than the transferred entity's, unless impracticable. BRPT's 2025 statements apply the 2012 text.

11. Business combinations across industries

Renewable, property and shipping companies. Single-asset companies (a permitted project, a building, a vessel) bought through their shares mostly fail the definition of a business or pass the concentration test, so no goodwill or deferred tax on the step-up arises. BRPT applied the test to PT Marina Indah Maritim (MIM) in 2024, whose fair value was "concentrated in the value of the vessel" (Note 1d, PDF p. 42).

Oil, gas and geothermal joint operations. Buying a participating interest in a joint operation that is a business is accounted for with the acquisition method's principles, including goodwill, under PSAK 111 (formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11) para. 21A.

Investment entities. A qualifying fund measures controlled investees at fair value through profit or loss, outside PSAK 103 (PSAK 110 para. 31).

BRPT's effective interest in ACE = (34.63% + 3.92% through its wholly owned Marigold) × 80% = 38.55% × 80% = 30.84%

That is roughly consistent with the 30.3 percent of group profit attributed to BRPT's owners.

Common control in BRPT's notes. On 1 October 2025 the group bought the 51 percent stakes of PT Buana Primatama Niaga (BPN) in PT Chandra Shipping International (CSI) and MIM, companies CAP already controlled (Note 1d, PDF pp. 41–42), and treated it as a common-control restructuring (Notes 29 and 31, PDF pp. 212, 216). BPN's "beneficial owner is the ultimate shareholder of CDI" (PT Chandra Daya Investasi Tbk, a CAP subsidiary; Note 45h, PDF p. 236), which fits para. 09.

Consideration = 87,625 + 73,350 = 160,975; carrying amount acquired = 161,296; difference = 321, credited to APIC

BRPT took Star Energy Group Holdings at carrying amounts in 2018 (Note 1d, PDF p. 52), and the Salak and Darajat goodwill from Star Energy's purchase from Chevron sits at 485,814 in both BRPT's Note 21 (PDF p. 141) and BREN's statements (272,016 + 213,798; BREN FS 2025, PDF p. 91).

Least-confident assertions

  • The CSI/MIM purchase fits PSAK 338's wording, since BPN's beneficial owner is CDI's ultimate shareholder (Note 45h), but three things stay open. The cash flow statement calls the 160,975 "additional investment in subsidiaries from non-controlling interest" (PDF p. 19). The paragraph sits in Note 31 Other equity components beside the NCI transactions. And the full 321 goes to BRPT's APIC although BRPT owns 38.55 percent of CAP, the buyer. That "ultimate shareholder of CDI" means BRPT's controlling shareholder is also read, not stated.

  • BRPT's SBE figures disagree within the FS. Note 43's table, BREN's statements (FY2024 PDF p. 82; FY2025 PDF pp. 77–78, 91) and BRPT's own SBE impairment test (Note 21, PDF p. 142: 85,020 = 78,709 − 5,740 + 12,051) use a customer contract of 78,709 and goodwill of 12,051. Note 43's text (12,333) and Note 21's cost roll-forward (customer contract 85,593 with different amortisation; goodwill addition 12,495 = 12,333 + OMI's 162) use other numbers. Section 7 uses the 78,709 and 12,051 set.

  • The book equity of 31,000 for SBE in section 7 is an assumption. BRPT does not disclose SBE's pre-acquisition carrying amounts, so the split of the excess between step-ups and goodwill is illustrative, though the fair values, goodwill and consideration are BRPT's.

  • Whether ACE's arbitration outcome will be a measurement-period adjustment depends on whether it reflects facts at 1 April 2025 and is settled by 1 April 2026; BRPT does not say. The 2026 interim statements were not checked.

  • That the Salak and Darajat goodwill entered BRPT at carrying amount under pooling is inferred from the identical 485,814 in BRPT's Note 21 and BREN's goodwill note; BRPT does not trace the goodwill through the 2018 combination.

presentation.deck: The theory of accounting for an acquisition from the definition of a business to pooling of interests, worked from Barito Pacific's 2025 purchases and set beside the industries where the boundary matters most
key_takeaways: A business combination is a transaction in which an acquirer obtains control of a business. Buying a set of assets that is not a business is an asset acquisition: the price is spread over the assets on relative fair values, and no goodwill or bargain purchase gain arises. The optional concentration test settles many cases quickly.

Under the acquisition method (PSAK 103) the acquirer measures the consideration and every identifiable asset and liability at acquisition-date fair value, including intangibles the seller never recorded. Goodwill is the residual. A negative residual is a bargain purchase gain in profit or loss, recognised only after the numbers have been rechecked. Provisional amounts may be corrected for up to one year.

When the same party controls both sides, nothing is bought from an outsider, so PSAK 338 replaces fair values with carrying amounts (pooling of interests) and puts the difference from the price in additional paid-in capital.

rows.title: Consolidation Procedures: the Worksheet and the Elimination Entries
rows.snippet: How a parent's books and a subsidiary's books become one set of group statements, entry by entry, worked from Barito Pacific's stake in Barito Renewables
rows.author: Dika Gustiana
rows.content:
In brief

  • Consolidated statements are never recorded in anyone's ledger. They are built on a worksheet that adds the parent's and the subsidiaries' statements line by line and then removes what is internal to the group: the parent's investment against the subsidiary's equity, intragroup balances, and intragroup income, expenses and dividends (PSAK 110 B86).

  • The elimination entries run in a fixed order. Reverse the parent's income from the subsidiary and the subsidiary's dividends, record the non-controlling interest's (NCI's) share, eliminate opening equity against the investment and opening NCI, allocate and depreciate the excess paid over book value, and cancel reciprocal balances. The worksheet has three parts, profit or loss, then retained earnings, then the balance sheet, each feeding the next.

  • The method the parent uses in its own books (cost or equity method, both allowed by PSAK 227) changes the first entry and adds one conversion entry, but never the consolidated result. A worksheet that balances can still be wrong, so the ties to the parent's equity and to NCI matter more than the totals.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) list each subsidiary's "total assets before elimination" in their 2025 statements. PT Barito Renewables Energy Tbk (BREN), 64.67 percent owned, has 3,867,410 at 31 December 2025, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF p. 26). What happens between such "before elimination" figures and the group's statements is the subject of this page.

After reading it a student should be able to prepare a three-part consolidation worksheet in the year of acquisition and in later years, write each elimination entry in order, adapt the worksheet to a parent that uses the cost method, and find the error when the worksheet does not balance.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's and BREN's statements are cited to their note; every other number is an illustration. Control, NCI measurement and profit attribution are taught in the Non-Controlling Interest essay and used here without re-deriving them.

1. The parent's own books decide what must be eliminated

The parent's investment in a subsidiary sits in its own books as one asset. How that asset is measured in the parent's separate financial statements (the parent's own statements, in which subsidiaries are investments) is a policy choice. PSAK 227 Separate Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 4, IAS 27) allows cost, PSAK 109 or the equity method, applied to each category of investment consistently (para. 10). The equity-method option was added in Indonesia by the amendment to PSAK 4 ratified in November 2015 and effective from 1 January 2016, following the 2014 IAS 27 amendment. Dividends from a subsidiary go to profit or loss under cost or PSAK 109, and reduce the investment under the equity method (para. 12).

The lecture notes (AKL Chapter 4) assume the parent uses the equity method "secara komplit", the complete equity method. The parent books its share of the subsidiary's profit after the depreciation of the excess it paid over book value, so its profit equals the consolidated profit attributable to its owners. Beams calls this one-line consolidation; the Long-Term Investments essay (section 5) explains the mechanism.

The running illustration. BRPT holds 64.67 percent of BREN (Note 1d). Its interest in BREN's geothermal business came through common-control transactions. BRPT acquired Star Energy Group Holdings (SEGHPL) in 2018, pooled as if combined from the start (Note 1d, PDF p. 52) at book values (policy Note 3e, PDF p. 70), and BREN acquired SEGHPL from BRPT in 2022 for new BREN shares (BREN FS 2025, Note 19b, PDF p. 115). No fair value excess arose at BRPT's level, although goodwill from Star Energy's earlier purchase of Salak and Darajat was carried across at its carrying amount; the Business Combinations essay (K1) covers both. To show every entry, suppose instead (illustration) that on 1 January 2024 BRPT had bought 65 percent of a geothermal company from outside owners. The notes call their subsidiary "Son"; this page calls it Sub. A fair value uplift is the amount by which an asset's fair value at acquisition exceeds its carrying amount in the subsidiary's books.

Consideration paid = 520,000

Sub's book equity = share capital 400,000 + retained earnings 200,000 = 600,000

Fair value uplifts: power plant +100,000 (20 years left, so 5,000 a year); spare-parts inventory +10,000 (used in 2024)

Identifiable net assets at fair value = 600,000 + 100,000 + 10,000 = 710,000

NCI at its proportionate share = 35% × 710,000 = 248,500

Goodwill = 520,000 + 248,500 − 710,000 = 58,500

Excess over book value = 520,000 + 248,500 − 600,000 = 168,500 = 100,000 + 10,000 + 58,500

PSAK 103 lets the acquirer choose fair value or the proportionate share for NCI, deal by deal (essay 25, section 2). The proportionate share is used here. Deferred tax on the uplifts is ignored to keep the steps short; K1 adds it.

Sub earns 90,000 and pays dividends of 40,000 in 2024, then earns 110,000 and declares dividends of 50,000 in 2025, of which 20,000 is still unpaid at year end.

The equity-method balance already contains the parent's share of Sub's retained profits and of the depreciated uplift. The cost-method balance contains neither, so the worksheet has to put them there before it can eliminate anything (section 6).

2. The worksheet has three parts, and each feeds the next

Each part of the worksheet ends in the figure the next part needs. The notes stack three parts (income statement, retained earnings statement, balance sheet), with columns for the parent, the subsidiary, the eliminations and the consolidated result.

  • Profit attributable to the owners of the parent, the last line of part one, is carried into part two.

  • Closing retained earnings, the last line of part two, is carried into part three.

  • Part three must then balance, total assets against total liabilities and equity.

PSAK 201 replaced the retained earnings statement with a statement of changes in equity, but the logic is unchanged. Every year starts again from the separate statements and repeats the entries for past events, such as the acquisition-date allocation.

PSAK 110 Consolidated Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) describes the three steps the entries perform (B86): combine like items of assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows; offset the parent's investment against its portion of the subsidiary's equity; and eliminate intragroup assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows in full. BRPT's policy repeats the third step: "All intragroup assets and liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows relating to transactions between members of the Group are eliminated in full on consolidation" (Note 3c, PDF p. 68).

3. The standard elimination sequence

The notes give six entries in a fixed order. Each removes something that would otherwise be counted twice.

Step

Problem it solves

Entry (equity-method parent)

(1) Income from subsidiary and dividends

The parent's income line repeats Sub's revenues and expenses; dividends to the parent move cash inside the group

Dr Income from Sub / Cr Dividends declared (Sub, parent's share); Cr Investment for the difference

(2) NCI share

Consolidated profit belongs partly to outside owners, and their dividends reduce their claim

Dr NCI share of profit / Cr Dividends declared (NCI's share); Cr NCI for the difference

(3) Opening equity against investment and NCI

Sub's opening equity is already represented by the investment and opening NCI

Dr Share capital and opening retained earnings (Sub), Dr Unamortised excess / Cr Investment (opening), Cr NCI (opening)

(4) Allocate the excess

The unamortised excess is a worksheet suspense account to be assigned to the assets it paid for

Dr Plant and equipment, Dr Goodwill (and inventory or cost of sales) / Cr Unamortised excess

(5) Depreciate the excess

Group depreciation follows acquisition-date fair values (PSAK 110 B88); Sub depreciates book values

Dr Depreciation / Cr Plant and equipment

(6) Reciprocal balances

Balances between group companies are neither assets nor liabilities of the group

Dr the payable / Cr the receivable; Dr intragroup income / Cr intragroup expense

Entries (1) and (2) together remove all of Sub's dividends. Entry (1) returns the investment to its opening balance, which is why entry (3) can eliminate it against opening equity. The intragroup profit eliminations of K3 and K4 can sit anywhere in the sequence without changing the result.

4. The year of acquisition

In the first year the opening equity in entry (3) is the equity at the acquisition date, and the inventory uplift reaches cost of sales because the spares were used during the year. For example (illustration), the 2024 worksheet for Sub:

(1) Dr Income from Sub 48,750 / Cr Dividends declared 26,000; Cr Investment in Sub 22,750

(2) Dr NCI share of profit 26,250 / Cr Dividends declared 14,000; Cr NCI 12,250

(3) Dr Share capital, Sub 400,000; Dr Retained earnings, Sub 200,000; Dr Unamortised excess 168,500 / Cr Investment in Sub 520,000; Cr NCI 248,500

(4) Dr Cost of sales 10,000; Dr Plant and equipment 100,000; Dr Goodwill 58,500 / Cr Unamortised excess 168,500

(5) Dr Depreciation 5,000 / Cr Plant and equipment 5,000

Entry (3) balances at 768,500 on each side. The investment, 520,000 + 48,750 − 26,000 = 542,750, is credited 22,750 + 520,000 = 542,750 and falls to zero. NCI closes at 248,500 + 12,250 = 260,750, which is 35 percent of Sub's net assets at group carrying amounts (book values plus the uplifts not yet written off).

35% × (600,000 + 90,000 − 40,000 + 100,000 − 5,000) = 35% × 745,000 = 260,750

Under the proportionate method goodwill is not part of NCI. Had control been obtained during the year, Sub's income and expenses would enter only from the acquisition date (B88), a case K5 takes up.

5. A later year: the full worksheet

From the second year on, entry (3) uses Sub's retained earnings at the start of the year and the excess still unamortised at that date. In 2025 three intragroup transactions also need entry (6).

  • On 1 July 2025 the parent lent Sub 30,000 at 6 percent a year. Half a year's interest, 30,000 × 6% × 6/12 = 900, is accrued by both and unpaid.

  • On 30 December Sub repaid 5,000 of the loan by bank transfer, which reached the parent on 2 January. Sub shows a loan payable of 25,000, while the parent still shows a receivable of 30,000. The 5,000 is cash in transit, money that has left one group company and not yet reached the other.

  • Sub's unpaid dividend of 20,000 includes 13,000 owed to the parent.

For example (illustration), the opening amounts for 2025:

Sub retained earnings, 1 Jan 2025 = 200,000 + 90,000 − 40,000 = 250,000

Unamortised excess, 1 Jan 2025 = 168,500 − 10,000 − 5,000 = 153,500 (plant 95,000 + goodwill 58,500)

Investment, 1 Jan 2025 = 542,750; NCI, 1 Jan 2025 = 260,750

(1) Dr Income from Sub 68,250 / Cr Dividends declared 32,500; Cr Investment in Sub 35,750

(2) Dr NCI share of profit 36,750 / Cr Dividends declared 17,500; Cr NCI 19,250

(3) Dr Share capital, Sub 400,000; Dr Retained earnings 1 Jan, Sub 250,000; Dr Unamortised excess 153,500 / Cr Investment in Sub 542,750; Cr NCI 260,750

(4) Dr Plant and equipment 95,000; Dr Goodwill 58,500 / Cr Unamortised excess 153,500

(5) Dr Depreciation 5,000 / Cr Plant and equipment 5,000

6. A parent on the cost method

A parent using the cost method reaches the same consolidated statements by changing two entries. Its investment still stands at 520,000, its opening retained earnings lack its share of Sub's retained profits, and its profit carries dividend income instead of the share of profit.

Parent's 2025 profit, cost method = 114,150 − 68,250 + 32,500 = 78,400

Conversion to equity basis at 1 Jan 2025 = 48,750 − 26,000 = 22,750

Parent's retained earnings, 1 Jan 2025, cost method = 400,000 − 22,750 = 377,250

Entry (0) lifts the investment to 520,000 + 22,750 = 542,750, the opening balance entry (3) eliminates, and lifts the parent's opening retained earnings to the equity-method 400,000. The 22,750 is the parent's share of Sub's retained profits since acquisition, 65% × (250,000 − 200,000) = 32,500, less its share of the excess already written off, 65% × 15,000 = 9,750. Entry (1) then removes only the dividend income, because the 68,250 share of profit was never in the parent's column, and the consolidated column comes out as in section 5. The notes cover only the equity method; this section follows Beams and PSAK 227.

7. Uniform policies and reporting dates

The worksheet adds like items only if they were measured alike and at the same date. PSAK 110 requires adjustments when a group member uses accounting policies other than the group's (B87). BRPT's policy says adjustments are made "when necessary ... to bring their accounting policies in line with the Group's accounting policies" (Note 3c, PDF p. 67). For example (illustration, separate from the section 5 worksheet), suppose Sub carries an office building it rents out at fair value under PSAK 240 (formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40), while the group uses the cost model. Sub bought the building on 1 January 2025 and booked a fair value gain of 3,000 at year end; the group's cost-model depreciation would be 400. Before the eliminations:

Dr Fair value gain 3,000; Dr Depreciation 400 / Cr Investment property 3,400

Like any adjustment to Sub's figures, its effect on profit is shared with NCI, so NCI's share of profit falls by 35% × 3,400 = 1,190.

Reporting dates should be the same. If that is impracticable, the subsidiary's most recent statements may be used, adjusted for significant transactions or events in between, provided the gap is no more than three months and the length of periods and the gap stay the same from period to period (B92–B93). The notes state the same three-month limit but only require material intervening events to be disclosed; PSAK 110 requires adjustment. For example (illustration), if Sub's year ended on 30 September and the parent lent it 10,000 on 15 November, Sub's statements would show no loan while the parent's showed a receivable. The adjustment comes first, then the elimination.

Adjust Sub: Dr Cash 10,000 / Cr Loan from parent 10,000

Eliminate: Dr Loan from parent 10,000 / Cr Loan to Sub 10,000

A subsidiary with another functional currency is first translated under PSAK 221 (formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21; see other-comprehensive-income).

8. Finding the error when the worksheet does not balance

Most errors show up in the balance sheet part, where totals stop agreeing; the notes advise checking each account one by one, but testing the entries first is faster.

  1. Each entry balances on its own. In the notes' own 2017 worksheet for Pam and Son, the equity elimination reads "Retained earnings $50.000; Capital stock – son $250.000; Unamortized excess $150.000 / Investment in Son $360.000; Noncontrolling interest $40.000". Debits are 450,000 and credits 400,000. Son's capital stock is 200,000; posted as written, the entry would leave the worksheet out by 50,000. The notes' worksheet itself uses 200,000.

  2. The investment and the subsidiary's equity accounts fall to zero.

  3. Each reciprocal pair cancels. Leave out entry (6a) in section 5 and the worksheet still balances. A loan to Sub of 5,000 survives in the consolidated column and cash is 5,000 short, an asset the group does not have in place of one it does.

  4. The ties hold. Consolidated profit and retained earnings attributable to owners equal the parent's under the equity method, and NCI equals its share of the subsidiary's net assets at group carrying amounts.

Check 4 catches errors that balance. The notes' Chapter 3 balance-sheet elimination one year after acquisition reads "Capital stock $60.000; Retained earnings $20.000; Goodwill $40.000 / Investment in son $108.000; Noncontrolling interest $12.000". It balances at 120,000, but Son's year-end retained earnings are 40,000 and goodwill on the notes' own figures is 20,000. Goodwill is overstated by 20,000 and 20,000 of Son's retained earnings survive into the consolidated column.

9. Consolidation procedures across industries

Groups in layers. A listed holding group can consolidate sub-group by sub-group. BREN's own statements already consolidate the Star Energy companies, so BREN's NCI can enter BRPT's worksheet as part of BREN's equity. Note 1d shows the chain, with PT Barito Wind Energy held 99.99 percent "through BREN" and PT Nefin Solar Asset 51 percent through Barito Wind Energy (PDF p. 26). K6 works through the effective interests.

Banks and structured entities. Banks consolidate securitisation vehicles and other structured entities, designed so that voting rights do not decide control, when the PSAK 110 control test is met; BRPT's policy also covers them (Note 3c, PDF p. 67).

Investment entities. An investment entity does not consolidate its investees, except subsidiaries that provide services for its investment activities, and measures them at fair value through profit or loss (PSAK 110 paras. 31–32).

Mining and oil and gas. A participating interest held under a joint operating agreement is usually a joint operation under PSAK 111 (formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11), and without joint control is still recognised line by line (para. 23), so there is no investment to eliminate and no NCI.

Islamic finance. A sharia subsidiary of a conventional bank is consolidated with the same entries, but it reports under PSAK 401 (formerly PSAK 101) with accounts such as murabahah receivables and temporary syirkah funds, which must be mapped to the group's chart of accounts first (STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED).

With no fair value excess at BRPT's level, NCI should be the outside share of BREN's book equity plus BREN's own NCI, which is what entry (3) and the NCI roll-forward produce. Least-confident assertions

  • The NCI residuals in section 10 (287 in 2025, (1,100) in 2024) are unexplained. They are too large for rounding of the ownership percentage, and BREN's 2025 treasury shares (6,000,000, 0.01 percent) are already in the computation. Separately, Note 34 gives BREN's 2024 total assets as 3,798,375, liabilities as 3,062,313 and profit as 158,612, while BREN's own audited 2024 figures, unchanged as comparatives in its 2025 FS and used in BRPT's Note 1d and 2024 segment note (Note 46, PDF p. 239), are 3,787,513, 3,054,980 and 155,083. The net-asset gap equals the profit gap (3,529), and BREN's 2025 FS have no restatement note. presentation.deck: How a parent's books and a subsidiary's books become one set of group statements, entry by entry, worked from Barito Pacific's stake in Barito Renewables
key_takeaways: Consolidated statements are never recorded in anyone's ledger. They are built on a worksheet that adds the parent's and the subsidiaries' statements line by line and then removes what is internal to the group: the parent's investment against the subsidiary's equity, intragroup balances, and intragroup income, expenses and dividends (PSAK 110 B86).

The elimination entries run in a fixed order. Reverse the parent's income from the subsidiary and the subsidiary's dividends, record the non-controlling interest's (NCI's) share, eliminate opening equity against the investment and opening NCI, allocate and depreciate the excess paid over book value, and cancel reciprocal balances. The worksheet has three parts, profit or loss, then retained earnings, then the balance sheet, each feeding the next.

The method the parent uses in its own books (cost or equity method, both allowed by PSAK 227) changes the first entry and adds one conversion entry, but never the consolidated result. A worksheet that balances can still be wrong, so the ties to the parent's equity and to NCI matter more than the totals.

rows.title: Intercompany Profit in Inventory: Downstream and Upstream
rows.snippet: Why a group earns nothing by selling to itself, how the worksheet defers and later releases the profit, who bears it when outside owners are present, and what deferred tax does to it, worked from Barito Pacific's 2025 numbers
rows.author: Dika Gustiana
rows.content:
In brief

  • A group earns revenue only when goods leave it. Consolidation therefore removes every intercompany sale and purchase in full, and removes the seller's profit on goods still held by another group company at year end, until those goods are sold to an outsider.

  • Who bears the deferred profit depends on direction. Profit on a downstream sale (parent to subsidiary) falls wholly on the parent's owners. Profit on an upstream sale (subsidiary to parent) belongs to a subsidiary that outside owners share in, so it is divided between the parent and the non-controlling interest (NCI).

  • The elimination changes the group's carrying amount of inventory but not its tax base, because Indonesian companies are taxed one by one. The difference is a deductible temporary difference under PSAK 212, so each deferral of profit carries a deferred tax asset at the buyer's tax rate, if the buyer expects taxable profit to use it.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) eliminated inter-segment revenue of 4,538 in 2025 (5,136 in 2024), in USD thousand, to arrive at consolidated revenue of 7,630,662 (BRPT FS 2025, Note 46, PDF p. 239). Its policy states that "all intragroup assets and liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows relating to transactions between members of the Group are eliminated in full on consolidation" (Note 3c, PDF pp. 67–68).

After reading this page a student should be able to eliminate intercompany sales and unrealised profit in a consolidation worksheet, release last year's deferral, attribute both between the parent and NCI, compute the parent's equity-method income, and add the deferred tax.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. Why the group cannot profit from selling to itself

A sale between two group companies moves goods from one pocket of the same owner to another, so from the group's point of view nothing has been sold. The lecture notes for AKL Chapter 5 justify the elimination by control over pricing, since the parent's management controls every intercompany transaction, "termasuk otorisasi dan penentuan harga" (including authorisation and pricing), and they treat the group as one reporting entity. A transfer price the parent sets itself cannot be evidence of value.

PSAK 110 Laporan Keuangan Konsolidasian (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) para. B86(c) requires the group to "eliminate in full intragroup assets and liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows", and adds that profits or losses on intragroup transactions "recognised in assets, such as inventory and fixed assets, are eliminated in full". Revenue in the consolidated statements is therefore earned only when a group company sells to an outside party, any entity that is not the parent or one of its subsidiaries.

The NCI essay (non-controlling-interest) covers how control is tested, how NCI is measured at acquisition and how profit, OCI and dividends are attributed to it. This page takes all of that as given and adds one complication. The subsidiary's profit "as the group sees it" excludes profit that is still sitting in another group company's warehouse.

2. Eliminating intercompany sales and purchases

Both group companies record an intercompany sale as if it were with an outsider, so the consolidated totals of sales and cost of sales are each overstated by the transfer price. The transfer price is the price one group company charges another.

For example (illustration), a parent sells goods that cost it 100,000 to its subsidiary for 120,000, a markup of 20 percent on cost. During the year the subsidiary sells goods that cost it 84,000 (at transfer price) to outside customers for 105,000. The remaining 36,000 is in its warehouse at year end.

Seller's books

Buyer's books

Purchase from outsider

Dr Inventory 100,000 / Cr Accounts payable 100,000

Intercompany sale

Dr Due from subsidiary 120,000 / Cr Sales 120,000; Dr Cost of sales 100,000 / Cr Inventory 100,000

Dr Inventory 120,000 / Cr Due to parent 120,000

Sale to outsiders

Dr Accounts receivable 105,000 / Cr Sales 105,000; Dr Cost of sales 84,000 / Cr Inventory 84,000

Gross profit in the separate books = (120,000 − 100,000) + (105,000 − 84,000) = 20,000 + 21,000 = 41,000

Group cost of goods sold to outsiders = 84,000 × 100 / 120 = 70,000

Group gross profit = 105,000 − 70,000 = 35,000

The first elimination removes the intercompany sale from both sides.

Dr Sales 120,000 / Cr Cost of sales 120,000

The entry is the same whatever happened to the goods afterwards. It changes no profit, only the size of the two lines. Without it, the group would report sales of 225,000 and cost of sales of 184,000, and 120,000 of that revenue, 53 percent, would be sales to itself. An unpaid balance of 120,000 would also be eliminated as a reciprocal balance (K2, entry (6)).

3. Unrealised profit in ending inventory

Removing the sale leaves a gap of 41,000 − 35,000 = 6,000 between the separate books and the group. That gap is the seller's profit on goods the buyer still holds. Profit on an intercompany sale is unrealised while the goods remain inside the group, and realised when a group company sells them to an outsider.

Ending inventory at transfer price = 36,000; at group cost = 36,000 × 100 / 120 = 30,000

Unrealised profit = 36,000 − 30,000 = 6,000

Dr Cost of sales 6,000 / Cr Inventory 6,000

After the first entry, consolidated cost of sales is 100,000 + 84,000 − 120,000 = 64,000. The debit brings it to 70,000, the group's cost of the goods sold to outsiders, and the credit brings inventory down to what the group paid outsiders. Consolidated inventory is then 30,000, measured at group cost, as PSAK 202 (formerly PSAK 14, IAS 2) requires for any inventory.

Markup on cost or margin on selling price. Intercompany pricing is usually quoted one of two ways, and confusing them misstates the elimination.

Markup on cost (20%)

Gross margin on selling price (20%)

Transfer price of 100 of cost

100 × 1.20 = 120

100 / 0.80 = 125

Unrealised profit as a share of the transfer price

20 / 120 = 16.67%

20%

Unrealised profit in 36,000 of ending inventory

36,000 × 16.67% = 6,000

36,000 × 20% = 7,200

The rule is that the unrealised profit is always computed on the ending inventory at transfer price, using the profit as a fraction of the transfer price. A markup m on cost converts to a margin of m / (1 + m), so 20 percent on cost is 16.67 percent of price.

4. Realising last year's deferral

Profit deferred at the end of one year is realised in the next, when the buyer sells the goods. The buyer's opening inventory still carries the transfer price, so its cost of sales this year is overstated by the profit eliminated last year.

For example (illustration), the subsidiary opened the year with a further 24,000 of goods bought from the parent at the same 20 percent markup, all sold during the year (their cost of sales is left out of section 3's figures).

Unrealised profit in opening inventory = 24,000 × 20 / 120 = 4,000

This year's worksheet starts from the separate books, which never saw last year's elimination, so the deferral has to be repeated against opening equity and then released through cost of sales. With the parent on the equity method (it carries the investment at cost plus its share of the subsidiary's profit, less dividends; section 6), last year's deferral sits in the parent's investment account, so the notes debit the investment for a downstream sale.

Dr Investment in subsidiary 4,000 / Cr Cost of sales 4,000

The credit lowers cost of sales, so this year's group profit rises by 4,000, the profit earned when the goods finally left the group. The debit restores the investment account, which the parent had reduced by 4,000 last year, so the later elimination of the investment against the subsidiary's equity balances. If the parent carries the subsidiary at cost in its separate statements, as PSAK 227 (formerly PSAK 4, IAS 27) allows, the same debit goes to opening retained earnings instead (K2 explains the difference).

Over two years the profit is not lost, only moved into the year the goods were sold outside.

5. Downstream and upstream sales

Direction decides who bears the elimination. A downstream sale runs from parent to subsidiary, so the unrealised profit sits in the parent's own profit and falls wholly on the parent's owners. An upstream sale runs from subsidiary to parent, so the unrealised profit sits in the subsidiary's profit, which outside shareholders share. The elimination of sales, cost of sales and inventory is the same in both cases. Only the attribution differs.

The starting numbers are BRPT's. BRPT owns 34.63 percent of PT Chandra Asri Pacific Tbk (CAP) directly and 3.92 percent through its wholly owned Marigold Resources (Note 1, PDF pp. 24 and 28).

Parent's effective interest = 34.63% + 3.92% = 38.55%; NCI = 100% − 38.55% = 61.45%

BRPT consolidates CAP despite holding under half of it because, it judges, the composition of CAP's Board of Directors gives it power over CAP's relevant activities and variable returns (Note 4, PDF p. 112). The NCI essay explains the control test.

CAP reported revenue of 7,020,007, expenses of 5,572,021 and profit of 1,447,986 for 2025, before intragroup eliminations (Note 34, PDF p. 221). Use that profit as the subsidiary's reported profit, and assume (illustration) that the parent's separate profit before investment income is 200,000 and that the section 2–4 sales run between the two, with opening unrealised profit of 4,000 and closing unrealised profit of 6,000.

Consolidated profit is the same, because the same 2,000 of net deferral (6,000 − 4,000) leaves the group either way. The split moves. Downstream, the parent's owners absorb all 2,000. Upstream, they absorb 38.55 percent of it, 771, and NCI absorbs 1,229, which is the 757,428 − 756,199 gap.

NCI share of profit (upstream) = NCI % × (subsidiary's reported profit + opening upstream unrealised profit − closing upstream unrealised profit)

What PSAK says about the split. PSAK 110 requires full elimination (B86(c)) and attribution of profit to the parent and NCI (B94), but does not say how an upstream elimination is attributed. The notes give the proportional method as the GAAP approach and mention an alternative of charging upstream profit wholly to the parent, as for downstream. IFRS 10 leaves the split to accounting policy. Proportional attribution is common, matches the notes and reflects that the profit being deferred is the subsidiary's, and this page and the NCI essay follow it.

6. The parent's equity method and the worksheet

Under the equity method the parent's own profit already equals the consolidated profit attributable to its owners, which is why the notes call it a one-line consolidation. The parent therefore has to make the same deferrals in its investment account.

Income from subsidiary = parent % × subsidiary's reported profit + opening unrealised profit released − closing unrealised profit deferred (downstream in full; upstream × parent %)

For the upstream case of section 5, the parent records:

Dr Investment in subsidiary 557,428 / Cr Income from subsidiary 557,428

Under PSAK the equity method is mainly a worksheet device for subsidiaries. In its separate statements a parent may carry a subsidiary at cost, under PSAK 109 or by the equity method (PSAK 227 para. 10).

The consolidation worksheet for the upstream case uses K2's numbering, with the profit eliminations between entries (5) and (6). The notes put them first; the order changes no total. This illustration has no fair value excess, so entries (4) and (5) are empty. Assume (illustration) that the parent's sales are 1,000,000, its cost of sales 700,000 and other expenses 100,000; that CAP's 5,572,021 of expenses splits into 5,000,000 of cost of sales and 572,021 of other expenses; and that the subsidiary paid no dividend.

Entry (5b) splits last year's deferral because the sale was upstream. The parent's 38.55 percent goes to the investment account and the NCI's 61.45 percent to opening NCI, since both were reduced when the profit was deferred; the notes' upstream example does the same with 32,000 and 8,000 at 80 percent. For a downstream sale, (5b) would debit the investment with the whole 4,000 and NCI would not appear.

7. Deferred tax on eliminated profit

The worksheet changes the group's carrying amount of inventory without changing anyone's tax position. BRPT states that "the Group is subject to income tax on an entity basis based on profit arising or derived from the tax jurisdiction in which the Group entities are domiciled and operates" (Note 23, PDF p. 145). Indonesia has no consolidated tax return, so the seller has already paid tax on the 6,000, and the buyer's tax base (the amount the tax authority will let it deduct) is the 36,000 it paid.

PSAK 212 Pajak Penghasilan (formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12) compares the consolidated carrying amount with that tax base. A carrying amount below the tax base is a deductible temporary difference, which gives a deferred tax asset (DTA), tax that will be recovered when the buyer sells the goods and deducts 36,000 against revenue the group sees as costing 30,000. PSAK 110 B86(c) points to it directly, saying the income-tax standard "applies to temporary differences that arise from the elimination of profits and losses resulting from intragroup transactions." The lecture notes leave tax out; Beams treats consolidated income taxes in a later chapter that the notes do not cover.

For example (illustration), both companies pay the general Indonesian corporate rate of 22 percent (whether CAP meets the listed-company conditions for 19 percent is not checked here).

Temporary difference = tax base 36,000 − carrying amount 30,000 = 6,000

DTA = 6,000 × 22% = 1,320

Dr Deferred tax asset 1,320 / Cr Income tax expense 1,320

Net reduction in group profit after tax = 6,000 − 1,320 = 4,680

The DTA is measured at the rate that will apply when the difference reverses, which is the buyer's rate, because the buyer holds the inventory and will take the deduction. When the two companies sit in different tax jurisdictions the seller's tax paid and the buyer's DTA no longer offset. CAP's group spans Indonesia and Singapore (Note 1, PDF p. 24). If the buyer were a Singapore company taxed at 17 percent:

DTA = 6,000 × 17% = 1,020; tax paid by the Indonesian seller = 1,320; difference left in tax expense = 300

Rates also differ inside Indonesia, and BRPT's own group shows it. Its geothermal JOC subsidiaries pay 34 percent (Note 23, PDF p. 145), so a DTA on inventory held by such a buyer would be 6,000 × 34% = 2,040. A listed company that meets the public-float conditions pays 3 points less than the general rate (19 percent), so the buyer's own status matters too.

Last year's deferral reverses with the goods. Its DTA of 4,000 × 22% = 880 was set up last year and is released this year, so for an upstream sale entry (5b) becomes:

Dr Investment in subsidiary 1,203 (38.55% × (4,000 − 880)); Dr NCI 1,917 (61.45% × 3,120); Dr Income tax expense 880 / Cr Cost of sales 4,000

Net effect on this year's group profit = −6,000 + 4,000 + 1,320 − 880 = −1,560

Upstream, NCI bears 61.45 percent of the after-tax effect and the parent 38.55 percent, so every percentage applied in section 5 is now applied to after-tax amounts. A DTA is recognised only if the buyer expects taxable profit to use it (PSAK 212 para. 24); BRPT, for instance, recognises none on the parent's fiscal losses (Note 41, PDF p. 225). A DTA can be offset only against a deferred tax liability of the same taxable entity, or of another entity that will settle net with the same authority, which Indonesia's entity-by-entity system rules out (PSAK 212 para. 74). That is why BRPT shows deferred tax assets of 122,742 and deferred tax liabilities of 263,652 for the CAP group side by side instead of netting them (Note 41, PDF p. 225).

US GAAP, which Beams follows, instead defers the seller's tax paid and forbids a buyer's-rate DTA on intra-entity inventory; PSAK has no such exception.

8. Intercompany losses that signal impairment

An intercompany sale below cost creates an unrealised loss, and the general rule eliminates it in the same way, by writing inventory back up to group cost. PSAK 110 B86(c) adds that "intragroup losses may indicate an impairment that requires recognition in the consolidated financial statements". If the loss exists because the goods are now worth less than they cost, the group would have had to write them down anyway under PSAK 202's lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV), so that part of the loss stays.

For example (illustration), a parent sells goods that cost it 10,000 to a subsidiary for 8,000. At year end they are still unsold and their NRV is 8,500.

Loss in the parent's books = 10,000 − 8,000 = 2,000

Write-down the group would recognise anyway = 10,000 − 8,500 = 1,500

Loss to eliminate = 8,500 − 8,000 = 500

Dr Inventory 500 / Cr Cost of sales 500

Consolidated inventory is 8,500, the lower of group cost of 10,000 and NRV of 8,500. Eliminating the whole 2,000 would carry the goods at 10,000, above what they can be sold for.

9. Intercompany profit across industries

Associates and joint ventures. An associate is an entity over which the investor has significant influence but not control, usually through a 20–50 percent holding, accounted for by the equity method. A sale to an associate is a sale to an outside party, because the associate is not in the group, so the revenue stays in full. Only the investor's share of the profit in goods still held is deferred (PSAK 228, formerly PSAK 15, IAS 28, para. 28). Losses that show a fall in NRV or an impairment are recognised in full for downstream sales and to the extent of the investor's share for upstream ones (para. 29).

The IASB's 2024 exposure draft on the equity method proposes recognising these gains and losses in full. The IASB was still deliberating in 2026, so this row may change.

Vertically integrated groups. Petrochemical producers moving olefins into polymer units, plantation groups selling crude palm oil to their own refineries, and coal miners supplying captive power plants all have large, recurring intercompany flows and inventory held at every stage. Segment reporting under PSAK 108 (formerly PSAK 5, IFRS 8) shows them when inter-segment revenue is part of the measure management reviews (para. 23(b)), together with the basis of accounting for transactions between segments (para. 27(a)).

Investment entities. A parent that qualifies as an investment entity does not consolidate its investees but measures them at fair value through profit or loss (PSAK 110 para. 31). Sales to those investees are then sales to outsiders and are not eliminated.

Transfer pricing. Consolidation eliminates the profit whatever the price, so an arm's-length tax adjustment to a transfer price changes current and deferred tax but not consolidated inventory, which stays at group cost.

The only inter-segment revenue comes from the property and other segments, and the note does not say what it is. At BRPT's level, then, the eliminations this page describes are close to zero.

They happen one level down. Each of the two large segments is a listed sub-group, and its own intragroup trade is eliminated before its figures reach BRPT.   • inventories-net: cost formulas and the lower of cost and NRV, which set the group cost in sections 3 and 8.

  • deferred-tax-assets: temporary differences and offsetting rules behind section 7.

  • long-term-investments: the equity method for associates in section 9.

  • revenues: when revenue is recognised, which here waits for the sale outside the group.

  • K1 Business Combinations; K2 Consolidation Worksheet (reciprocal balances, cost versus equity method); K4 Intercompany Plant Assets (the same logic for land and depreciable assets, including BRPT's elimination of a land gain between CAP and SRI); K5 Consolidated Cash Flows; K6 Mutual Holdings.

Least-confident assertions

  • B86(c) and B94 require full elimination and attribution but do not say how an upstream elimination is split, so it is an accounting-policy choice. Proportional attribution is common and is used here; the notes' alternative (all to the parent) is not ruled out by the text.

  • The source of BRPT's inter-segment revenue (property and others) and of the eliminations of 29 in segment result and 139,079 in segment assets is not explained in Note 46. That CAP's segment carries large intra-segment eliminations is an inference from its structure (Indonesian plants, a Singapore refinery and trading companies in Note 1), not a disclosed figure.

  • Treating BREN's eliminated revenue of 7,205 as mostly holding-company charges to the operating companies rests on the segment table alone. BREN's tax-line elimination of 998 could be deferred tax on eliminated profit or something else, and is not used here.

  • Measuring the DTA at the buyer's rate follows IAS 12's reversal principle as firms explain it; IAS 12 does not state the rule for this case in so many words. The 22 percent and 19 percent Indonesian rates and the 17 percent Singapore rate are from knowledge; only the 34 percent JOC rate is taken from BRPT (Note 23), and whether CAP qualifies for 19 percent was not checked.

  • The IASB's 2024 equity-method exposure draft may change PSAK 228 para. 28; the IASB decided in October 2025 to do further work and had not concluded by mid-2026. The current text was checked only through secondary sources. Where a downstream deferral goes when the associate (SRI) is carried at nil is a judgement BRPT does not disclose.

presentation.deck: Why a group earns nothing by selling to itself, how the worksheet defers and later releases the profit, who bears it when outside owners are present, and what deferred tax does to it, worked from Barito Pacific's 2025 numbers
key_takeaways: A group earns revenue only when goods leave it. Consolidation therefore removes every intercompany sale and purchase in full, and removes the seller's profit on goods still held by another group company at year end, until those goods are sold to an outsider.

Who bears the deferred profit depends on direction. Profit on a downstream sale (parent to subsidiary) falls wholly on the parent's owners. Profit on an upstream sale (subsidiary to parent) belongs to a subsidiary that outside owners share in, so it is divided between the parent and the non-controlling interest (NCI).

The elimination changes the group's carrying amount of inventory but not its tax base, because Indonesian companies are taxed one by one. The difference is a deductible temporary difference under PSAK 212, so each deferral of profit carries a deferred tax asset at the buyer's tax rate, if the buyer expects taxable profit to use it.

rows.title: Intercompany Profit on Plant Assets: Land, Depreciable Assets and Piecemeal Realisation
rows.snippet: How a group removes the gain one of its companies books when it sells land, equipment or buildings to another, and how that gain comes back as depreciation, as an outside sale, or through leases and bonds, with Barito Pacific's 2025 statements as the starting numbers
rows.author: Dika Gustiana
rows.content:
In brief

  • When one group company sells a plant asset to another above its carrying amount, the seller books a gain the group has not earned, because the asset has not left the group. Consolidation removes the gain in full and puts the asset back at the seller's carrying amount, the group cost.

  • For land the gain stays eliminated until the land is sold outside the group. For a depreciable asset the buyer depreciates the transfer price, so each year's excess depreciation is corrected, and the gain comes back piece by piece over the remaining life.

  • Direction decides who bears the gain. A downstream sale (parent to subsidiary) falls wholly on the parent's owners; an upstream sale (subsidiary to parent) is shared with the non-controlling interest (NCI). Intercompany leases and bonds bought back within the group follow the same logic.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) report property, plant and equipment, net, of 5,660,112 at 31 December 2025 against 3,489,851 a year earlier, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, statement of financial position, PDF p. 14). Inside that group, PT Krakatau Chandra Energi (KCE) completed a land sale and purchase with PT Chandra Asri Alkali (CAA) and PT Chandra Cilegon Port (CCP) during 2025 for 26,223 (Note 45h, PDF p. 237). All three are subsidiaries of PT Chandra Asri Pacific Tbk (CAP), which BRPT consolidates (Note 1d, PDF pp. 24–25), and BRPT's policy is that intragroup transactions "are eliminated in full on consolidation" (Note 3c, PDF p. 68).

After reading this page a student should be able to eliminate an intercompany gain on land and depreciable assets in the year of transfer, in later years and on sale outside, split it between the parent and NCI, and treat intercompany leases and bond holdings the same way.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. Why an intercompany transfer creates a gain the group has not earned

A group earns a gain on an asset only when the asset leaves the group. PSAK 110 Laporan Keuangan Konsolidasian (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) requires profits and losses on intragroup transactions recognised in assets such as inventory and fixed assets to be eliminated in full (para. B86(c)), because for the economic unit nothing has changed.

The lecture notes (AKL Chapter 6) start from the same point. A transfer above book value creates an unrealised gain, recorded by the seller but not earned by the group, which must be removed from the consolidated statements and, where the parent uses the equity method (the investment at cost plus its share of the subsidiary's profit, less dividends), from the parent's own income from subsidiary. The notes call the equity method a "one-line consolidation" (AKL Chapter 2): it must give the parent the same profit as full consolidation, condensed into one line.

NCI, the worksheet and depreciation itself come from earlier essays (section 11). Inventory (K3) works the same way; the difference is time. An inventory gain usually comes back within a year, a gain on equipment over its remaining life, and a gain on land only if the land is sold outside.

2. Land: the gain is eliminated until the land is sold outside

Land is not depreciated (PSAK 216 Aset Tetap, formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16, para. 58), so nothing in the buyer's books ever corrects the gain. The consolidation entry has to remove it in the year of sale and put it back on the worksheet every year until the land leaves the group.

The notes add "paten yang memiliki masa manfaat yang tidak terbatas" to this class, but a patent has a finite legal life. The class is land and intangibles with an indefinite useful life, which PSAK 238 (formerly PSAK 19, IAS 38) does not amortise.

For example (illustration), take BRPT's 26,223 as the transfer price. Parent P owns 70 percent of subsidiary S, the same percentage CDI holds in KCE (Note 1d). The seller carried the land at 16,223.

Gain in the seller's books = 26,223 − 16,223 = 10,000

Group cost of the land = 16,223, whoever holds it

Year of sale. The worksheet entry is the same in both directions; what differs is whose profit carried the gain.

Later years. The holder still carries the land at 26,223 and the seller's retained earnings still contain the gain, so each year's worksheet repeats the elimination against opening equity, which under P's equity method sits in the investment account.

The notes print the upstream entry "Investment in Sun $18.000 / Noncontrolling interest share $2.000 / Land $20.000" among the 2016 entries, introduced only by "Apabila Pop memutuskan untuk menggunakan tanah tersebut". It is the later-years entry: in the year of sale the gain is still in the income statement, and the notes' own 2016 worksheet debits "Gain on sale". The debit is also to the opening NCI balance, not to NCI share, which is the income-statement line.

Sale outside the group. Suppose the holder sells the land to an outside buyer for 30,000.

Holder's gain = 30,000 − 26,223 = 3,777

Group's gain = 30,000 − 16,223 = 13,777

P's books mirror it (Dr Investment in S / Cr Income from subsidiary, 10,000 or 7,000), and in the upstream case 3,000 of the 13,777 group gain goes to NCI.

3. Depreciable assets: the gain comes back through depreciation

A depreciable asset corrects itself slowly. The buyer depreciates the transfer price, the group should depreciate the group cost, and correcting the difference each year releases a slice of the gain into consolidated profit, the piecemeal recognition of the notes and Beams.

For example (illustration), on 1 January 2025 one company sells equipment to the other. BRPT depreciates machinery and heavy equipment straight-line over 4–37 years (Note 3n, PDF p. 90); take five years remaining, no residual value.

Seller's cost 50,000, accumulated depreciation 20,000, carrying amount 30,000

Transfer price 40,000; gain = 40,000 − 30,000 = 10,000

Buyer's depreciation = 40,000 / 5 = 8,000 a year

Group's depreciation = 30,000 / 5 = 6,000 a year

Depreciation correction = 8,000 − 6,000 = 2,000 a year = 10,000 / 5

At the end of 2025 the buyer carries 40,000 − 8,000 = 32,000 and the group 30,000 − 6,000 = 24,000; the 8,000 gap is the gain not yet realised.

Year of transfer. Two entries.

(a) Dr Gain on sale of equipment 10,000 / Cr Equipment 10,000

(b) Dr Accumulated depreciation 2,000 / Cr Depreciation expense 2,000

Consolidated equipment, net, is 30,000 − 6,000 = 24,000. Entry (a) is the notes' net form. The gross form restores the seller's cost and accumulated depreciation (Dr Gain 10,000, Dr Equipment 10,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 20,000), showing 50,000 less 26,000 at year end, also 24,000, and closer to what the group would disclose had the transfer never happened. The notes describe it in words but name no account for the 10,000 debit, which is Equipment.

Year-end transfers. A sale on 31 December needs only entry (a) that year; correction (b) starts the next.

4. Downstream and upstream: who bears the gain

The elimination entries are the same in both directions; the split between the parent's owners and NCI is not. A downstream gain is the parent's own, so NCI share is computed on the subsidiary's reported profit. An upstream gain is part of the subsidiary's profit, so the parent bears its percentage and NCI the rest.

The notes put this as "unrealized profit yang harus dieleminasi juga sebesar kepemilikan parent". That holds for the parent's equity-method income. On consolidation the whole gain is eliminated in both directions (PSAK 110 para. B86(c)), and only its allocation is proportional.

For example (illustration), continue the equipment case with P owning 70 percent of S. In 2025 S reports profit of 60,000 and P's own profit, before income from S, is 100,000; the 10,000 gain sits with the seller.

Downstream (P sells)

Consolidated profit is the same; only its attribution moves. In the downstream case the 2,000 correction goes wholly to P, because the excess depreciation in S's books comes from P's gain. The notes' upstream truck example gives 80% × 50,000 + 80% × 1,000 − 80% × 3,000 = 38,400 by the same formula. It lists the truck's remaining life as "5 years" but depreciates "÷ 3 years", and the investment reaches 80 percent of S's equity three years after the sale, so three years is the consistent figure.

The check. Suppose S's equity was 200,000 at the start of 2025, P bought its 70 percent at book value, and no dividends were paid, so S's equity is 260,000 at year end.

Upstream: P's investment = 140,000 + 36,400 = 176,400 = 70% × 260,000 − 70% × 8,000

Upstream: NCI = 60,000 + 15,600 = 75,600 = 30% × (260,000 − 8,000)

Downstream: P's investment = 140,000 + 34,000 = 174,000 = 70% × 260,000 − 8,000; NCI = 30% × 260,000 = 78,000

The investment account always equals the parent's share of the subsidiary's book equity less the unrealised gain it bears, which is how the notes reconcile the investment in their combined example: 540,000 less 5,000 and 14,400 gives 520,600.

5. Later years and the sale outside the group

From the second year the gain has left the income statement and sits in opening retained earnings, so the worksheet removes it from opening equity and continues the depreciation correction. With the parent on the equity method, the opening debit goes to the investment account (downstream) or to the investment account and NCI (upstream).

For example (illustration), the worksheet at 31 December 2026 for the equipment case. The unrealised gain at the start of the year is 8,000, and accumulated depreciation has to be cut by two years of correction, 4,000.

Downstream

Upstream

Each side totals 12,000. In P's books, Dr Investment in S / Cr Income from subsidiary, 2,000 downstream or 1,400 upstream, repeats each year to 2029.

If the parent keeps the investment at cost in its separate statements, as PSAK 227 Laporan Keuangan Tersendiri (formerly PSAK 4, IAS 27) allows, the opening debits go to its opening retained earnings instead (K2).

Sale outside the group. Suppose the buyer sells the equipment to an outsider on 31 December 2027 for 25,000.

Buyer's carrying amount = 40,000 − 3 × 8,000 = 16,000; buyer's gain = 25,000 − 16,000 = 9,000

Group's carrying amount = 30,000 − 3 × 6,000 = 12,000; group's gain = 25,000 − 12,000 = 13,000

Unrealised at the start of 2027 = 10,000 − 2 × 2,000 = 6,000: 2,000 through depreciation, 4,000 as extra gain
