The asset has left both ledgers, so no asset account is touched, and nothing remains to eliminate.

The notes' combined Pam–Sun example (three transfers at once) recomputes cleanly: income from Sun 90% × 80,000 + 5,000 + 90% × 4,000 − 32,000 + 4,000 = 52,600, NCI share 10% × 84,000 = 8,400. Its NCI entry is reversed. The notes write "Noncontrolling interest $8.400 / Dividends $3.000 / Noncontrolling interest share $5.400"; it should be Dr NCI share 8,400 / Cr Dividends 3,000; Cr NCI 5,400.

6. Sideways sales, losses and deferred tax

Sales between two subsidiaries. A sideways (lateral) sale is treated like an upstream sale from the seller's side: the gain is eliminated in full and borne by the seller's owners, the parent's effective share and the seller's NCI. BRPT's KCE–CAA/CCP land sale is of this kind. Note 45h names KCE first and Note 16 (PDF p. 137) shows KCE holding investment-property land, so KCE is the likely seller, though the note does not say so. BRPT owns 34.63 percent of CAP directly and 3.92 percent through Marigold, 38.55 percent in all, which it treats as control because CAP's board composition gives it power over CAP's relevant activities (Note 4, PDF p. 112; see non-controlling-interest on control with less than a majority). CAP holds CDI at 60 percent; CDI holds KCE at 70 percent and CSP at 99.99 percent; CSP holds CCP at 100 percent; CAP holds CAA through CAP2 at 99.99 percent (Note 1d, PDF pp. 24–25).

BRPT's effective interest in KCE = 38.55% × 60% × 70% = 16.19%

BRPT's effective interest in CAA = 38.55% × 100% × 99.99% = 38.55%

BRPT's effective interest in CCP = 38.55% × 60% × 99.99% × 100% = 23.13%

For example (illustration), if KCE were the seller and the gain were 10,000, BRPT's owners would bear 16.19% × 10,000 = 1,619 of the elimination and the NCI at the three levels the other 8,381. Had CAA or CCP sold, BRPT's owners would bear about 3,855 or 2,313. The Mutual Holdings essay (K6) works the layered allocation.

Losses. A loss on an intercompany sale is eliminated the same way with the signs reversed, unless the price shows the asset has lost value. PSAK 110 para. B86 adds that intragroup losses may indicate an impairment that must be recognised in the consolidated statements. For example (illustration), equipment carried at 30,000 is sold within the group for 22,000. If its recoverable amount under PSAK 236 (formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36), the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, is also 22,000, the 8,000 loss is an impairment the group would have booked anyway, and it stays; otherwise it is eliminated.

Deferred tax. The notes do not mention tax. The buyer's tax base, the amount the tax authority lets it deduct, is the transfer price, while the consolidated carrying amount is the group cost. The gap is a deductible temporary difference, one that lowers future taxable profit, under PSAK 212 Pajak Penghasilan (formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12). For example (illustration), with a 22 percent rate, the equipment case at the end of 2025:

Temporary difference = 32,000 tax base (tax depreciation of 8,000 assumed equal to book) − 24,000 group carrying amount = 8,000

Deferred tax asset = 22% × 8,000 = 1,760; Dr Deferred tax asset 1,760 / Cr Income tax expense 1,760

The asset unwinds by 22% × 2,000 = 440 a year as the gain is realised. PSAK 212 measures it at the buyer's rate, and PSAK 110 para. B86(c) sends these differences to PSAK 212. Indonesian land transfers bear a 2.5 percent final tax on the gross price (PP 34/2016), outside PSAK 212's mechanics. That tax is paid to the state, so it is a real group expense and is not eliminated (about 656 on 26,223 if fully taxable); the land elimination itself usually carries no deferred tax.

7. Intercompany leases

An intragroup lease is not a lease for the group, which owns and uses the asset. Under PSAK 116 Sewa (formerly PSAK 73, IFRS 16) the lessee books a right-of-use (ROU) asset and a lease liability at the present value of the payments, then depreciation and interest, while the lessor of an operating lease keeps the asset and books rental income. Consolidation removes the lessee's side and the rental income, leaving the asset and its depreciation in the lessor's books.

BRPT's property segment (building and hotel management) earned 4,505 of inter-segment revenue in 2025, eliminated with 33 from "others" (Note 46, PDF p. 239); the note does not say whether it is rent.

For example (illustration), take 4,505 as an annual rent, paid in arrears for five years, discounted at 8 percent.

Present value = 4,505 × (1 − 1.08⁻⁵) / 0.08 = 4,505 × 3.99271 = 17,987.2

Lessee's year 1: depreciation = 17,987.2 / 5 = 3,597.4; interest = 8% × 17,987.2 = 1,439.0; total expense 5,036.4

Lessee's year-end balances: lease liability = 17,987.2 × 1.08 − 4,505 = 14,921.1; ROU asset = 17,987.2 − 3,597.4 = 14,389.7

Dr Rental income 4,505.0, Dr Lease liability 14,921.1 / Cr ROU asset 14,389.7, Cr Depreciation expense 3,597.4, Cr Interest expense 1,439.0

Both sides total 19,426.1. Consolidated profit in year 1 is 5,036.4 − 4,505.0 = 531.4 above the two companies' combined profit, because the lessee's front-loaded expense goes with the lessor's flat income; over five years the differences net to zero. An intragroup sale and leaseback is eliminated the same way: no gain, no ROU asset, and the asset stays at group cost.

8. Intercompany bonds: constructive retirement

When one group company buys another's bonds from outside holders, the group has retired its own debt, and consolidation books a gain or loss the issuer never recorded. The owner's notes have no AKL Chapter 7 (in Beams, Intercompany Profit Transactions — Bonds), so this section follows Beams and PSAK 109 Instrumen Keuangan (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9). PSAK 109 says a debt repurchased by its issuer is extinguished (para. B3.3.2) and the difference between its carrying amount and the price paid goes to profit or loss (para. 3.3.3). The consolidated statements therefore show a constructive gain or loss on retirement, one that exists only in the group's view, in the year of purchase.

For example (illustration), BRPT issued Rp 400 billion of Series A shelf-registration bonds in July 2025, equivalent to 24,487 (Note 1c, PDF p. 24). Take a simplified USD version: P has bonds with face value 20,000 outstanding, an 8 percent coupon paid each 31 December, and an unamortised discount of 400 with four years left. On 1 January S, 70 percent owned, buys half of them in the market for 10,300.

Carrying amount of the half in P's books = 10,000 − 200 = 9,800

Constructive loss = 10,300 − 9,800 = 500

The interest lines then no longer cancel. Following Beams, discount and premium are amortised straight-line.

P's interest expense on the half = 800 + 200 / 4 = 850

S's interest income = 800 − 300 / 4 = 725

Difference = 850 − 725 = 125 a year = 500 / 4

Year of purchase, at 31 December:

Dr Bonds payable 10,000, Dr Interest income 725, Dr Loss on constructive retirement 500 / Cr Unamortised discount 150, Cr Interest expense 850, Cr Investment in bonds 10,225

Consolidated profit is 500 − 125 = 375 below the combined profit.

Next year, the unrealised loss is 500 − 125 = 375 at the start:

Dr Bonds payable 10,000, Dr Interest income 725, Dr Investment in S 375 (where P's equity-method entries carried the loss) / Cr Unamortised discount 100, Cr Interest expense 850, Cr Investment in bonds 10,150

Beams assigns the whole constructive gain or loss to the issuer, here P, so NCI is unaffected; if S were the issuer, its NCI would share it. PSAK 109 does not settle that allocation. And PSAK 109 requires the effective interest method, not straight-line; the total of 500 is the same, only its timing across the four years differs.

9. Intercompany asset transfers across industries

Power and utilities. An in-house contractor's margin on a plant built for a group power producer is an intercompany profit on a depreciable asset, released over the plant's life, which BRPT sets at 20–30 years (Note 3n). The deferred margin, and any deferred tax asset on it, stays in the consolidated balance sheet for decades.

Property. When a developer sells land from its inventory to a group hotel or rental subsidiary, the group eliminates the revenue and margin and reclassifies the land to fixed assets or investment property (PSAK 240, formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40) at the developer's cost.

Mining. Heavy equipment sold to a group mine and depreciated on units of production releases the gain with output rather than with time.

Associates and joint ventures. Under PSAK 228 Investasi pada Entitas Asosiasi dan Ventura Bersama (formerly PSAK 15, IAS 28) para. 28, the investor recognises gains on upstream and downstream transactions only to the extent of unrelated investors' interests, so it eliminates only its own share. The IASB has proposed full recognition instead (ED/2024/7); redeliberations began in October 2025.

10. Presentation and analysis: Barito Pacific's Notes 3c, 14, 45 and 46

A correct elimination makes the transaction disappear, so BRPT's FS show four traces only.

The land sale. KCE, CAA and CCP are all consolidated, so the 26,223 should leave the group's land at its original cost, and it leaves no visible trace. The place to look is KCE's investment-property land (Note 16, PDF p. 137), which moved only by translation, from 16,622 to 16,507 (Note 16b, PDF p. 135). The note names neither the seller nor any gain.

The associate. PT Synthetic Rubber Indonesia (SRI) is 45 percent owned through CAP. The group's share of SRI's net assets is 7,044 (45% × 15,652, rounded), against an 11,440 land-gain elimination and a carrying amount of nil, which the note explains. SRI's 2025 profit share, 45% × 16,965 = 7,634, is disclosed as unrecognised, because the elimination exceeds the group's share of net assets, so the interest stays at zero until cumulative profits cover the 11,440 (policy, Note 3, PDF p. 86). On that reading the balancing "excess" row should be 11,440 − 7,044 = 4,396 (2024: 11,440 + 592 = 12,032), not the 11,440 printed, a presentation slip. If 11,440 is the 45 percent share under PSAK 228 para. 28, the whole gain was 11,440 / 45% = 25,422, a reading of the arithmetic.

The segments. The four segments add to 203,474 + 93,449 + 1,623 + 980 = 299,526, and the elimination column takes consolidated depreciation up to 308,865. Correcting depreciation on intercompany gains lowers group depreciation (on losses it raises it), as section 3 showed, so a positive 9,339 must be dominated by something else, most likely depreciation of fair value uplifts from acquisitions recorded only at group level. The note does not show how much intercompany asset profit, if any, the column contains.

11. Related essays

  • fixed-assets-net: depreciation methods, useful lives and impairment, which this page corrects rather than re-teaches.

  • non-controlling-interest: NCI measurement and attribution, used in sections 2–5.

  • right-of-use-assets-net and lease-liabilities-non-current: the lessee's side of PSAK 116, eliminated in section 7.

  • deferred-tax-assets: the temporary difference on eliminated gains.

  • long-term-investments: associates and the PSAK 228 partial elimination.

  • K1 (business combinations), K2 (the worksheet and elimination order), K3 (intercompany inventory), K5 (consolidated cash flows), K6 (mutual holdings and layered allocation).

Least-confident assertions

  • The seller in the KCE–CAA/CCP land sale is probably KCE (Note 16) but not stated, and the seller's gain is not disclosed. The effective interests (16.19, 38.55 and 23.13 percent) use year-end Note 1d percentages; CAP's stake in CDI fell from 70 to 60 percent in 2025, and at 70 percent the effective interest in KCE would be 18.89 percent.

  • The "excess of share of losses" row in Note 14 repeats 11,440 where 4,396 (2024: 12,032) would balance. The treatment is clear from the unrecognised-profit disclosure, so the row is read as a presentation error. In 2013–14 the IFRS Interpretations Committee favoured eliminating the full share and presenting any excess as a deferred gain; the IASB's narrow-scope amendment was never finalised, and BRPT floors the interest at nil instead.

  • Reading the positive 9,339 depreciation elimination in Note 46 as acquisition fair value depreciation is inference. BRPT does not explain the column, and the 4,505 of property inter-segment revenue may not be rent.

  • That the land elimination carries no deferred tax rests on reading final tax (PP 34/2016) as outside PSAK 212's scope. The 22 percent rate ignores the reduced rate some listed companies qualify for.

  • Allocating a constructive bond gain or loss wholly to the issuer follows Beams. PSAK 109 is silent on the allocation to NCI, and other textbooks split it between issuer and holder.

presentation.deck: How a group removes the gain one of its companies books when it sells land, equipment or buildings to another, and how that gain comes back as depreciation, as an outside sale, or through leases and bonds, with Barito Pacific's 2025 statements as the starting numbers
key_takeaways: When one group company sells a plant asset to another above its carrying amount, the seller books a gain the group has not earned, because the asset has not left the group. Consolidation removes the gain in full and puts the asset back at the seller's carrying amount, the group cost.

For land the gain stays eliminated until the land is sold outside the group. For a depreciable asset the buyer depreciates the transfer price, so each year's excess depreciation is corrected, and the gain comes back piece by piece over the remaining life.

Direction decides who bears the gain. A downstream sale (parent to subsidiary) falls wholly on the parent's owners; an upstream sale (subsidiary to parent) is shared with the non-controlling interest (NCI). Intercompany leases and bonds bought back within the group follow the same logic.

rows.title: Consolidated Cash Flows and Mid-Year Acquisitions: NCI Dividends, Cash Acquired and Preacquisition Earnings
rows.snippet: How a group builds one cash flow statement out of many companies, where the non-controlling interests and the deals that change the group land in it, and what happens to a subsidiary's results before the day it was bought, worked through Barito Pacific's 2025 statements
rows.author: Dika Gustiana
rows.content:
In brief

  • A consolidated cash flow statement reports only cash that crosses the group's boundary. Cash moving between parent and subsidiary is eliminated, so of a subsidiary's dividend only the part paid to the non-controlling interests (NCI) survives, as a financing outflow. In the indirect method the reconciliation starts from consolidated profit, NCI's share included, and deducts the profit of equity-accounted investees (associates and joint ventures carried at the investor's share of their net assets) that was not received in cash.

  • Deals that change the group are classified by what they do to control. Obtaining or losing control of a subsidiary is one investing line, net of the subsidiary's own cash acquired or given up (PSAK 207 paras. 39 and 42). Buying from or selling to the NCI while control continues is financing (para. 42A). The acquired company's balances never pass through operating cash flows.

  • A subsidiary bought during the year enters the consolidated income statement and cash flow statement from the acquisition date. The lecture notes' second approach, consolidating the full year and deducting "preacquisition earnings", is no longer allowed. Its only remnant is a note disclosure of the acquiree's revenue and profit since acquisition and on a full-year pro forma basis (PSAK 103 para. B64(q)).

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) paid dividends of 60,121 to the NCI of its subsidiaries in 2025, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, consolidated statement of cash flows, PDF p. 19). Its largest acquisition of the year, Aster Chemical and Energy Pte. Ltd. (ACE), was completed on 1 April 2025, a quarter into the year.

After reading this page a student should be able to prepare a consolidated cash flow statement by the indirect and direct methods, classify every cash flow that involves the NCI or a change in the group, and consolidate a subsidiary bought or partly sold in the middle of a year.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The order follows the lecture notes for AKL Chapter 4 (the cash flow part) and Chapter 8 (acquisitions during the period). How NCI is measured and how ownership changes are recorded in equity is in the Non-Controlling Interest essay (25-non-controlling-interest); this page takes those entries as given and follows the cash.

1. One entity, one cash pool

The group reports as if it were one company, so its only cash flows are flows with parties outside the group. The notes open the topic with the "single concept" of cash and cash equivalents, defined as in PSAK 207 Statement of Cash Flows (formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7) and covered in 08-cash-and-cash-equivalents. BRPT's policy states the consequence: all cash flows "relating to transactions between members of the Group are eliminated in full on consolidation" (Note 3c, PDF p. 68).

Adding up each company's statement and removing intragroup flows gives the same answer as the notes' route, which derives the statement from the consolidated balance sheets and income statement.

The intragroup dividend shows why elimination matters. For example (illustration), parent P owns 80 percent of S, and S pays a dividend of 50.

In S's own statement: financing outflow (50)

In P's own statement: dividend received 80% × 50 = 40, operating or investing

Added together: 40 − 50 = (10)

Eliminate the 40 that stayed inside the group: consolidated financing outflow (10), dividends paid to NCI

Only the 10 paid to the NCI left the group, and only that remains in the consolidated statement.

2. The indirect method: from consolidated profit to operating cash

Under PSAK 207 the reconciliation starts from profit before attribution, so NCI's share of profit is never "added back" (paras. 18(b) and 20). The indirect method removes items that did not involve cash and adjusts for changes in working capital. The notes' example is Pop Corporation and an 80 percent-owned subsidiary, with consolidated profit of 200 for 2017, of which 150 is the controlling share and 50 is NCI's, and cash rising from 180 to 255. The notes start from the controlling share and add the NCI share back, since it increases consolidated net assets "persis seperti" the controlling share. That layout reflects older US practice, where minority interest was deducted as if it were an expense. Both reach the same figure.

Net increase = 165 + 10 − 100 = 75; cash 180 + 75 = 255

Only the cash part of an investee's profit stays in operating cash. Pop's income from its equity investee is 15, but only the 10 received as dividends was cash, so the notes deduct the "undistributed income" of 5. Dividends received may be classified as operating or investing, consistently from period to period (paras. 31 and 33). If Pop chose investing, the whole 15 comes out of the reconciliation and the 10 appears below.

Operating = 165 − 10 = 155; investing = 10 + 10 = 20; net increase still 75

The notes leave a non-cash purchase undisclosed. Their balance sheets show equipment rising from 600 to 800 after depreciation of 100, so 800 − 600 + 100 = 300 of equipment was added, and a note payable due 2019 of 300 appears where there was none. No cash line covers either, which fits equipment bought with the note, though the notes do not say so. PSAK 207 keeps such transactions out of the statement and requires them to be disclosed elsewhere (para. 43); BRPT does this in its Note 44.

NCI is reconciled, not reported. NCI moves from 80 to 110, that is 80 + 50 − 20. The 50 is non-cash attribution and the 20 is a financing outflow. Nothing about NCI belongs in operating cash flows except the profit inside the starting figure.

3. The direct method

The direct method lists gross receipts and payments, so the NCI does not appear in operating activities at all. The notes rebuild Pop's 2017 operating cash flow from the same statements.

Cash received from customers = sales 750 − increase in receivables 105 = 645

Dividends received from equity investee = 10

Cash paid to suppliers = cost of goods sold 300 + increase in inventories 45 + decrease in payables 20 = 365

Paid to employees 54, other operating expenses 47, interest 24

Net cash from operating activities = 645 + 10 − (365 + 54 + 47 + 24) = 655 − 490 = 165

PSAK 207 encourages the direct method (para. 19). BRPT uses it (Note 3b, PDF p. 67), so its operating section runs from receipts from customers of 7,939,631 to net operating cash of 309,608, and its profit attributable to NCI appears nowhere in the statement.

4. Cash flows with the non-controlling interests

Every cash flow between the group and its NCI is a transaction with owners, so it belongs in financing. That covers three kinds of flow.

Event

Consolidated classification

Basis

Subsidiary pays dividends to NCI

Financing outflow

Para. 34 permits financing or operating; the notes use financing

Subsidiary issues new shares to NCI

Financing inflow

Para. 17, contributions from owners

Parent buys shares from NCI, or sells shares to new NCI, control kept

Financing outflow or inflow

Paras. 42A–42B

A parent's purchase of more shares in a subsidiary is an investing outflow in its separate statements. In the consolidated statements it is a payment to one class of the group's own owners, since the subsidiary's assets were already fully consolidated. European enforcers required an issuer that had shown such a purchase in investing to move it to financing (ESMA, decision EECS/0119-01).

For example (illustration), P buys a further 10 percent of S from the NCI for 12,000 and keeps control.

P's separate statement: investing outflow (12,000), acquisition of investment in subsidiary

Consolidated statement: financing outflow (12,000), acquisition of non-controlling interest

Equity: NCI falls by its carrying amount for 10 percent; the difference goes to equity attributable to the parent (essay 25, section 5)

The reverse runs through the same activity. When a subsidiary issues shares to new NCI, the cash is a financing inflow even though the parent's percentage falls. Take BRPT's subsidiary PT Chandra Daya Investasi Tbk (CDI) as the starting point. It issued shares to Phoenix Power B.V. for 95,000 (Note 31, PDF p. 217) and listed on the stock exchange in July 2025, raising 77,036 + 68,428 − 3,880 of issue costs = 141,584 (Note 1, PDF p. 36). Together they cut CAP's interest in CDI from 70 to 60 percent. Both are financing inflows; BRPT shows the second as "proceeds from limited public offering of a subsidiary".

BRPT's line for subscriptions by NCI, 367,032, can be largely split from Note 1, though BRPT does not split it (inference). Glencore subscribed 146,690 for its 20 percent of CAPGC on 26 March 2025 (PDF p. 43), Phoenix paid 95,000, and the remaining 367,032 − 146,690 − 95,000 = 125,342 is close to BPN's pro-rata share of the capital injected into CSI and MIM on 1 October 2025 (section 9). The Glencore money came in at CAPGC, the company that bought ACE a week later, so NCI financing paid for part of an investing outflow.

5. Obtaining control: one investing line, net of cash acquired

When the group buys a subsidiary it acquires that company's assets and liabilities in one transaction, and PSAK 207 presents the whole transaction as a single investing line (para. 39). The amount is the cash paid less the cash and cash equivalents the subsidiary already held (para. 42), because that cash comes into the group with it. The note must disclose the total consideration, the part paid in cash, the cash in the subsidiary, and the other assets and liabilities by major category (para. 40).

BRPT's acquisition of ACE gives every element (Note 43, PDF p. 227). The consideration is provisional, meaning the price is still subject to final adjustment, here through arbitration with the seller.

Provisional consideration = 671,970

Less deferred consideration, not yet paid = 283,225

Cash paid on acquisition = 671,970 − 283,225 = 388,745

Less ACE's cash and cash equivalents acquired = 215,431

Net cash outflow = 388,745 − 215,431 = 173,314

With 6,377 for Aster Polymer Solutions Pte. Ltd. (APS), bought on 1 August (13,076 paid less 6,699 acquired, PDF p. 229), the investing line is 173,314 + 6,377 = 179,691. The 283,225 still owed is a non-cash investing transaction in Note 44 (PDF p. 235). IAS 7 does not say how its later payment is classified. Practice varies between investing, financing and a split, and IASB staff proposed in September 2026 that deferred consideration with the character of a borrowing be financing.

The acquired balances bypass operating activities. A statement built from consolidated balance sheets must strip out the balances that arrived with the subsidiary, or their arrival looks like operating activity. Take BRPT's inventories as the starting point: 398,837 at the end of 2024 and 1,273,619 at the end of 2025 (statement of financial position, PDF p. 14), with 970,281 acquired through ACE and 39,608 through APS (Note 43, PDF pp. 226 and 228).

Change on the balance sheet = 1,273,619 − 398,837 = 874,782 increase

Inventories acquired = 970,281 + 39,608 = 1,009,889

Change from operations = 874,782 − 1,009,889 = 135,107 decrease

Read naively, the balance sheet suggests 874,782 tied up in stock. With the acquisitions removed, inventories released 135,107 of cash (ignoring write-downs and translation). Likewise ACE's acquired property, plant and equipment of 1,604,141 is not capital expenditure.

Bargain purchase gains bring no cash. A bargain purchase arises when the identifiable net assets acquired are worth more than the price. ACE's were valued at 2,444,134 against consideration of 671,970, a gain of 1,772,164; APS added 95,875 (108,951 − 13,076). BRPT's income statement shows 1,868,039 of such gains (PDF p. 17). An indirect reconciliation deducts all of it, and in BRPT's direct statement it never appears. How a bargain purchase is tested belongs to K1.

6. Losing control and the full map of ownership events

Losing control mirrors obtaining it: one investing line, the proceeds received net of the cash the former subsidiary takes out of the group (paras. 39 and 42).

For example (illustration), continue essay 25's subsidiary: net assets of 425,000 including cash of 35,000 (an assumption for this page), goodwill 60,000, NCI 170,000. The parent sells 40 percent for 230,000 cash and keeps 20 percent, worth 115,000, as an associate.

Gain on loss of control = (230,000 + 115,000 + 170,000) − (425,000 + 60,000) = 30,000

Investing inflow = 230,000 − 35,000 = 195,000, disposal of subsidiary, net of cash disposed

Retained 20 percent at 115,000, and the gain of 30,000: non-cash, removed in the indirect method

Had the subsidiary held more cash than the sale raised, the line would be a net investing outflow. Cash flows from obtaining and losing control are not offset against each other (para. 41).

7. Acquisitions during the year: preacquisition earnings

A subsidiary's income before the acquisition date was earned for its former owners and was paid for in the purchase price. The notes call it preacquisition earnings, and the dividends paid out of it before that date preacquisition dividends.

The notes' example has Pop buying 90 percent of Sun for 427,500 on 1 April 2016. (The notes write Son, Sun and Pam for the same companies, and the first column of their table reads "Jan 1 – Mar 1" where the quarter ends on 31 March.)

Sun's profit: 1 January–31 March 25,000; 1 April–31 December 75,000; year 100,000

Sun's dividends: before 1 April 20,000; after 30,000

Sun's equity at 1 April = 470,000 + 25,000 − 20,000 = 475,000

Cost = 90% × 475,000 = 427,500, so there is no excess to allocate

Approach 2 overstates sales by 50,000. The notes describe two ways to exclude preacquisition earnings: leave Sun's revenue and expenses before 1 April out of the consolidated income statement, or include Sun's full year and deduct "preacquisition earnings" as a separate line. They describe the second only in words; the column below is computed here from their data.

Approach 1: from acquisition date

Approach 2: full year less preacquisition earnings (computed here)

Sales

600,000 + 150,000 = 750,000

600,000 + 200,000 = 800,000

Expenses

400,000 + 75,000 = 475,000

400,000 + 100,000 = 500,000

Preacquisition earnings

none

(25,000)

Consolidated profit

275,000

275,000

NCI share, 10% × 75,000

The bottom line agrees; the top line does not. PSAK 110 Consolidated Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) includes a subsidiary's income and expenses only from the date control is gained (para. B88), and BRPT's policy says so in nearly the same words (Note 3c, PDF p. 67). Approach 1 is the only one allowed. Approach 2 was the method ARB 51 called "usually" preferable (para. 11) until FAS 160 amended it. The notes' own worksheet already follows approach 1, eliminating Sun's first-quarter sales of 50,000 and cost of sales of 25,000.

PSAK measures NCI on the acquisition date. The notes measure NCI from 1 January, 10% × 470,000 plus 10% of the first quarter's profit, 49,500, and give NCI 10 percent of the full year's dividends, 5,000, of which 2,000 was paid before Pop arrived. PSAK 103 Business Combinations (formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3) measures NCI at the acquisition date, here at its share of net assets because book value equals fair value.

NCI at acquisition = 10% × 475,000 = 47,500

NCI at 31 December = 47,500 + 7,500 − 10% × 30,000 = 52,000

Notes' route: 49,500 + 7,500 − 5,000 = 52,000

Check: 10% × Sun's equity at year end of 520,000 = 52,000

The closing figure agrees, but the 2,000 of dividends paid in the first quarter is not a group transaction. It reduced Sun's net assets before the acquisition and so reduced the price. Under PSAK the worksheet eliminates Sun's equity at the acquisition date.

Dr Capital stock 400,000; Dr Retained earnings at 1 April 75,000 / Cr Investment in Sun 427,500; Cr NCI 47,500

Dr Income from Sun 67,500 / Cr Dividends 27,000; Cr Investment in Sun 40,500

The second entry corrects the notes, which print "Dividend $18.000 / Investment in Son $49.500". Pop received 90% × 30,000 = 27,000 after the acquisition, and the notes' own worksheet carries 27,000 and 40,500, which is what clears Pop's investment of 427,500 + 67,500 − 27,000 = 468,000.

Sun's cash enters through the acquisition line. The consolidated cash flow statement follows the income statement: Sun's flows count from 1 April, and the purchase is one investing line. For example (illustration), if Sun held cash of 60,000 on 1 April:

Investing outflow = 427,500 − 60,000 = 367,500

Dividends to NCI in financing = 10% × 30,000 = 3,000, not the notes' 5,000

B64(q) moves preacquisition results into the notes. Leaving the first quarter out makes the year hard to compare with the next, so PSAK 103 para. B64(q) asks for the acquiree's revenue and profit since the acquisition date, and the group's revenue and profit pro forma, that is, recomputed as if the acquisition had happened at the start of the year. BRPT gives both for ACE (Note 43, PDF pp. 227–228).

ACE since 1 April: revenue 4,634,352, loss 337,222

Group pro forma for 2025: revenue 8,735,677, profit 1,589,142, against reported 7,630,662 and 1,615,634

Pro forma less reported: revenue 1,105,015 higher, profit 26,492 lower

A part-sale is recorded on the day it happens. The notes' Chapter 8 also lets a parent that sells 10 percent of a 90 percent subsidiary on 1 April record the sale as if it happened on 1 January. PSAK 110 attributes profit by the ownership actually held, so the sale is recorded on 1 April. With the subsidiary's profit of 36,000 for the year, the NCI share is 36,000 × (10% × 3/12 + 20% × 9/12) = 900 + 5,400 = 6,300, not 7,200, and the credit to the parent's equity is 40,000 − 32,900 = 7,100, not 8,000. The 40,000 received is a financing inflow either way.

8. Consolidated cash flows across industries

Investment entities do not report acquisitions net of cash. A venture capital fund or similar entity that meets PSAK 110's investment-entity definition does not consolidate its investees but measures them at fair value through profit or loss (para. 31). Buying an investee is then an investing purchase of a financial asset, and para. 42A does not apply to its stakes.

Asset acquisitions in a corporate wrapper still use the para. 39 line. Concessions, plantation land and power projects are often bought by buying the company that holds them. If the company is not a business under PSAK 103, the purchase is an asset acquisition, with no goodwill or bargain purchase, but the buyer still obtains control of a subsidiary. BRPT's wind subsidiary bought 51 percent of PT Lombok Timur Bayu Energi and PT Sukabumi Bayu Energi in January 2024 as asset acquisitions, and their cash outflows of 3,373 and 4,055 are shown as investing activities (Note 43, PDF pp. 232–233).

Joint-venture investors show large non-cash deductions. Equity-accounted ventures in property and infrastructure contribute profit without cash.   • non-controlling-interest: NCI measurement, attribution and the equity entries for ownership changes.

  • long-term-investments: equity-accounted associates and joint ventures.

  • other-equity-component and additional-paid-in-capital: where differences from transactions with NCI and common-control restructurings sit.

  • K1: consideration, deferred consideration, bargain purchase, asset acquisitions and PSAK 338.

  • K2: the elimination entries this page's worksheet steps rely on.

  • K6: effective interests in multi-layer groups such as BRPT–CAP–CAPGC.

Least-confident assertions

  • The CSI/MIM classification is a judgement with support on both sides. That BPN's capital injection of about 138,000 sits in the 367,032 financing inflow is inference; BRPT does not split that line, and the US dollar amount of the CSI injection depends on the rate applied to the deed's rupiah figure.

  • The split of 367,032 into Glencore 146,690, Phoenix 95,000 and about 125,342 from BPN is inference. The BPN residual matches its pro-rata injection less the 11,623 of shares issued by converting payables (Note 44) only to within about 1,250.

  • The CDI dates conflict inside the FS. Note 31 dates the Phoenix issue 14 March 2025 and attributes the whole fall from 70 to 60 percent to it; Note 1 shows the 14 March deed raising authorised capital, the issue to Phoenix on 11 April (to 66.67 percent) and the IPO in July (to 60.0 percent). This page follows Note 1.

  • That the ACE pro forma difference reflects ACE's first quarter assumes the pro forma adds only that quarter with no other adjustments. BRPT does not explain how it was compiled.

  • The inventory calculation in section 5 ignores write-downs, translation and measurement-period changes to ACE's provisional figures, so 135,107 approximates the operating movement; BRPT does not report it.

presentation.deck: How a group builds one cash flow statement out of many companies, where the non-controlling interests and the deals that change the group land in it, and what happens to a subsidiary's results before the day it was bought, worked through Barito Pacific's 2025 statements
key_takeaways: A consolidated cash flow statement reports only cash that crosses the group's boundary. Cash moving between parent and subsidiary is eliminated, so of a subsidiary's dividend only the part paid to the non-controlling interests (NCI) survives, as a financing outflow. In the indirect method the reconciliation starts from consolidated profit, NCI's share included, and deducts the profit of equity-accounted investees (associates and joint ventures carried at the investor's share of their net assets) that was not received in cash.

Deals that change the group are classified by what they do to control. Obtaining or losing control of a subsidiary is one investing line, net of the subsidiary's own cash acquired or given up (PSAK 207 paras. 39 and 42). Buying from or selling to the NCI while control continues is financing (para. 42A). The acquired company's balances never pass through operating cash flows.

A subsidiary bought during the year enters the consolidated income statement and cash flow statement from the acquisition date. The lecture notes' second approach, consolidating the full year and deducting "preacquisition earnings", is no longer allowed. Its only remnant is a note disclosure of the acquiree's revenue and profit since acquisition and on a full-year pro forma basis (PSAK 103 para. B64(q)).

rows.title: Mutual Holdings and Complex Group Structures
rows.snippet: How a group attributes profit when its companies own each other, from connecting affiliates to subsidiaries holding parent shares, worked through Barito Pacific's layered geothermal and petrochemical chains
rows.author: Dika Gustiana
rows.content:
In brief

  • In a complex structure, control decides which companies are consolidated, and the effective interest decides how their profit and net assets are split. The effective interest is found by multiplying percentages down each ownership path and adding the paths together. A company can be a subsidiary while the parent's effective interest in it is below 50 percent.

  • When companies own each other, each one's profit depends on the other's, so the split needs simultaneous equations. The equations add mutual profit twice. Only the shares held by outsiders, multiplied by each equation's result, add back to the group's total profit.

  • When a subsidiary holds shares of its parent, Beams offers two treatments, the treasury stock approach and the conventional approach. PSAK 232 treats parent shares held by any group member as treasury shares, deducted from equity at cost, so the treasury stock approach is the one that fits Indonesian standards. Holdings between subsidiaries are eliminated, and there is no treasury alternative for them.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) report non-controlling interests (NCI) of 3,802,216 at 31 December 2025, against total equity of 6,045,632, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, statement of financial position, PDF p. 16). Outside shareholders own 62.9 percent of the group's equity and took 1,125,827 of the year's profit of 1,615,634, or 69.7 percent (PDF p. 17), because BRPT reaches its geothermal plants through six or seven layers of companies, some partly owned, some owning the same company from two directions. It controls Chandra Asri with an effective interest of 38.55 percent.

After reading this page a student should be able to compute effective interests in any chain, allocate profit through connecting affiliates with unrealised profits, solve the equations for mutual holdings, choose between the treasury stock and conventional approaches, and read a group's ownership table.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note and PDF page. Every other number is an illustration, or comes from the lecture notes' examples, labelled as such.

1. Direct and indirect holdings: recap and effective interest

An indirect holding works by the same consolidation procedure as a direct one, once each company's profit is restated on an equity basis from the bottom up. The father–son–grandson chain of AKL Chapter 9, section A, is covered in the Non-Controlling Interest essay (FSLI 25, section 7). Pop owns 80 percent of Son and Son owns 70 percent of Toy. Toy's profit is allocated to Son first, then Son's enlarged profit to Pop.

Pop's profit on an equity basis = 100,000 + 80% × 50,000 + 80% × 70% × 40,000 = 162,400

The effective interest is the share of a company's profit and net assets that finally reaches a given owner. It follows two rules.

Along one path: multiply the percentages

Across several paths into the same company: add the products

BRPT owns 64.67 percent of PT Barito Renewables Energy Tbk (BREN), which owns all of Star Energy Group Holdings Pte. Ltd. (SEGHPL). SEGHPL reaches Star Energy Geothermal Salak, Ltd. (SEG-SL) through a chain in which BREN reports its own effective interest as 80.91 percent (BREN FS 2025, Note 1, PDF p. 18; BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF pp. 24–27).

BRPT's effective interest in SEG-SL = 64.67% × 80.91% = 52.32%

The other 47.68 percent belongs to two groups of outsiders: those inside BREN's group (100% − 80.91% = 19.09%) and BREN's own outside shareholders (35.33% × 80.91% = 28.59%). The three shares add to 100 percent.

Control is a separate test, and it travels down the chain whole. PSAK 110 Laporan Keuangan Konsolidasian (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) asks whether the investor has power, exposure to variable returns and the link between them. BRPT controls BREN, BREN controls SEGHPL, and so on down. Each subsidiary of a subsidiary is a subsidiary of BRPT, at whatever effective interest the multiplication gives. Consolidation brings in 100 percent of SEG-SL's assets, and the effective interest only decides how its profit is split between BRPT's owners and the NCI.

2. Connecting affiliates

In a connecting-affiliate structure the allocation has to start from the bottom company, because profit reaches the parent by two routes at once. The term means that the parent and one of its subsidiaries both hold shares in the same company. The notes' example (section B) has Pet owning 70 percent of Sal and 60 percent of Tai, and Sal owning 20 percent of Tai. The problem is order. Tai's profit must reach Sal before Sal's profit can reach Pet, so the schedule starts with the company nobody else in the group sits below.

BRPT's own structure contains one. Star Energy Geothermal Holdings (Salak-Darajat) B.V. (Holdings BV) is owned 51 percent by Star Energy Geothermal Pte. Ltd. (SEGPL) and 49 percent by Star Energy Geothermal Netherlands B.V. (SEG-NBV). SEGHPL owns 90 percent of SEGPL and 100 percent of SEG-NBV (BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF pp. 26–27).

SEGHPL's effective interest in Holdings BV = 90% × 51% + 100% × 49% = 45.9% + 49.0% = 94.9%

BREN's table shows 94.90 percent for Holdings BV (PDF p. 18), so the rule reproduces the company's own figure.

The allocation schedule with unrealised profits. Intercompany profits are removed before anything is allocated, and they are charged to the company that recorded them. Profit sitting in a buyer's inventory or land has not yet been earned from outsiders (K3, K4). 3. Parent shares held by a subsidiary

Parent shares held by a subsidiary are, for the group, shares it has bought back from itself. A mutual holding exists when two affiliated companies each hold shares in the other. The first case in the notes (section C) is a subsidiary owning shares of its parent. From the group's view those shares are not outstanding. The group has bought back part of itself, and the question is how to show that and how to split profit.

In the notes' example Pam buys 90 percent of Son on 1 January 2016 for 540,000, when Son's equity is 600,000 (capital 400,000, retained earnings 200,000), so there is no goodwill. Son buys 10 percent of Pam on 5 January 2016 for 140,000, when Pam's equity is 1,400,000 (capital 1,000,000 in shares of 10 par, retained earnings 400,000). Separate profits for 2016 are 100,000 for Pam and 60,000 for Son, with no dividends.

The treasury stock approach treats Pam's shares held by Son as if Pam had bought them back. Son's investment in Pam is reclassified to treasury shares at cost and deducted from consolidated equity, and the mutual holding is otherwise ignored in profit. Son has no income from Pam in 2016.

Pam's income from Son = 90% × 60,000 = 54,000; Pam's profit = 100,000 + 54,000 = 154,000

NCI share = 10% × 60,000 = 6,000; NCI at year end = 10% × (600,000 + 60,000) = 66,000

The conventional approach treats Pam's shares held by Son as constructively retired, and lets Son's outside owners share in Pam's profit through Son's 10 percent stake. Then neither company's profit on an equity basis can be found first, because each includes a share of the other. The notes solve it with two equations.

P = 100,000 + 0.9S

Converting retained earnings. The notes reuse the same equations to put two years of undistributed earnings onto an equity basis. The separate increases in net assets from 2016 to 2017 are 196,000 for Pam (100,000 + 120,000 − 60,000 + 36,000 received) and 106,000 for Son (60,000 + 80,000 − 40,000 + 6,000 received).

P = 196,000 + 0.9S; S = 106,000 + 0.1P, so P = 320,219.78 and S = 138,021.98

To Pam's retained earnings: 90% × 320,219.78 = 288,197.80; to NCI: 10% × 138,021.98 = 13,802.20

Which approach PSAK permits. PSAK 232 Instrumen Keuangan: Penyajian (formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) para. 33 deducts the cost of an entity's own equity instruments that it reacquires from equity, records no gain or loss on their purchase, sale, issue or cancellation, and states that such shares may be acquired and held by the entity "or by other members of the consolidated group". PSAK 110 para. B86 eliminates intragroup equity in full. Together they make the parent's shares held by a subsidiary treasury shares of the group, shown at cost as a deduction. That is the treasury stock approach's presentation, and it rules out the conventional approach's balance sheet, with capital cut to 900,000 and retained earnings to 360,000 as if the shares were cancelled. Para. 33 does not say whether Son's NCI shares in Pam's profit through those shares, so the conventional profit split is a question PSAK leaves open. Earnings per share follow the presentation. Under PSAK 233 (formerly PSAK 56, IAS 33) the 10,000 shares held by Son are not outstanding, so 2016 earnings per share are 154,000 / 90,000 = 1.711, ignoring the four days before Son's purchase, against 152,307.69 / 90,000 = 1.692 under the conventional split.

A second attribution point is open as well. Beams gives NCI 10 percent of Son's whole 2017 profit of 86,000, including the 6,000 dividend received from Pam. On a strict group view that dividend is not income, so NCI's share of profit would be 10% × 80,000 = 8,000, and the 600 by which the dividend enlarges NCI's claim would be a transfer within equity from the parent's owners. NCI ends at 70,600 either way. PSAK gives no explicit guidance on this split.

In Indonesia the case is rare. UU 40/2007 on limited companies art. 36(1) forbids a company to issue shares to be owned by itself or by another company whose shares it owns directly or indirectly. Shares obtained by operation of law, gift or bequest are exempt (art. 36(2)) but must be transferred within one year (art. 36(3)). BRPT's FS show no subsidiary holding BRPT shares. PT Barito Pacific Lumber, which holds 0.58 percent, belongs to Prajogo Pangestu, not to the group (Note 28, PDF p. 211; Note 45, PDF p. 235). BRPT's treasury shares of 1,600 consist of shares the Company bought back itself (Note 30, PDF pp. 212–213).

4. Subsidiaries that hold each other

When two subsidiaries own each other, the treasury stock approach has nothing to work on, because neither holding is in the parent. The notes' case (section D): Pam owns 80 percent of Set, Set owns 70 percent of Ton, and Ton owns 10 percent of Set. Set's outside owners hold the remaining 10 percent and Ton's hold 30 percent. Separate profits for 2018, excluding income from affiliates, are 112,000 for Pam, 51,000 for Set and 40,000 for Ton. Three companies give three equations.

P = 112,000 + 0.8S

S = 51,000 + 0.7T

T = 40,000 + 0.1S

Solving the pair that loops first:

S = 51,000 + 0.7 × (40,000 + 0.1S) = 79,000 + 0.07S

0.93S = 79,000; S = 84,946.24

T = 40,000 + 0.1 × 84,946.24 = 48,494.62

P = 112,000 + 0.8 × 84,946.24 = 179,956.99

Pam's shares are held only by its own shareholders, so P is the controlling share. NCI is each subsidiary's outside percentage times its equation result:

NCI in Set = 10% × 84,946.24 = 8,494.62

NCI in Ton = 30% × 48,494.62 = 14,548.39

Check: 179,956.99 + 8,494.62 + 14,548.39 = 203,000 = 112,000 + 51,000 + 40,000

B86), so Set's NCI is the outside 10 percent only. The equations remain the arithmetic for attributing profit.

The notes' goodwill is grossed up from the parent's price. The notes give goodwill of 25,000 on Pam's 260,000 for 80 percent of Set's 300,000 equity, and 10,000 on Set's 112,000 for 70 percent of Ton's 150,000. Both gross up the price: 260,000 / 80% − 300,000 = 25,000. PSAK 103 Kombinasi Bisnis (formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3) para. 19 measures NCI at its own fair value, which also gives full goodwill but not by grossing up a price that includes a control premium, or at its share of net assets. Under the second option goodwill would be 260,000 − 80% × 300,000 = 20,000 and 112,000 − 70% × 150,000 = 7,000.

6. Complex structures across industries

Banks and structured entities. A bank may consolidate a securitisation vehicle or a fund in which it owns no shares at all, because PSAK 110 tests control through power and variable returns, not equity. Its effective equity interest may be zero, and the vehicle's equity is then NCI or, if redeemable, a liability (FSLI 25 section 9).

Investment entities. A parent that qualifies as an investment entity does not consolidate its subsidiaries; it measures them at fair value through profit or loss (PSAK 110 para. 31), except subsidiaries that provide investment-related services (para. 32). A venture fund's layered portfolio companies therefore never enter a chain calculation. A non-investment parent above it still consolidates everything, including what the fund holds (para. 33).

Conglomerate pyramids and the two-shareholder rule. Indonesian groups stack listed companies, as BRPT does with BREN, CAP and Chandra Daya Investasi, and many subsidiaries carry a small stake held by a sister company to keep two shareholders. Each listed layer adds outsiders, and each small stake is NCI in a sub-group's statements but not in the group's.

Least-confident assertions

  • Reading BRPT's Note 1d is partly inference. The table gives direct holdings for Holdings BV (51 and 49 percent) but apparently effective ones elsewhere (90 percent for SEG-WW, which BREN reports as its effective interest). The ACEHI row shows "indirect ownership through ACEHI 19.80" while BREN shows ACEHI as an NCI holder. Linking the 4.80 percent to SEGHPL's 24.24 percent of ACEHI rests on the arithmetic matching BRPT's 80.91 percent statement. BRPT's table also gives 80.19 percent for Holdings BV's stake in SEGSDBV and no 2024 figure for the ACEHI row, although the ACEHI shares were registered in December 2023; the page uses BREN's 80.20 percent, the only figure that reproduces 80.91.

  • That BRPT holds the 5 percent "direct ownership" of SEGSS and DGI is read from BRPT's table wording and from BREN's matching effective percentages. BREN names Barito Pacific as the holder only for SEGI and SEGH.

  • How to attribute a parent's dividend paid to a subsidiary with NCI (Beams' 8,600 in profit, against 8,000 in profit plus a 600 equity transfer) is not settled by PSAK. PSAK 232 para. 33 settles presentation (treasury shares) but not whether Son's NCI shares in the parent's profit, so the conventional profit split, and this dividend point, remain policy choices.

  • UU 40/2007 art. 36 bans issuing shares to a cross-holder. Whether a subsidiary may buy existing parent shares on the market is not settled by its text, and secondary sources read it differently.

  • The 287 difference between BRPT's NCI in BREN and BREN's two layers has no disclosed explanation, and the split of the 153,883 bridge in section 7 between outsiders below CAP and parent-level items is not disclosed.

presentation.deck: How a group attributes profit when its companies own each other, from connecting affiliates to subsidiaries holding parent shares, worked through Barito Pacific's layered geothermal and petrochemical chains
key_takeaways: In a complex structure, control decides which companies are consolidated, and the effective interest decides how their profit and net assets are split. The effective interest is found by multiplying percentages down each ownership path and adding the paths together. A company can be a subsidiary while the parent's effective interest in it is below 50 percent.

When companies own each other, each one's profit depends on the other's, so the split needs simultaneous equations. The equations add mutual profit twice. Only the shares held by outsiders, multiplied by each equation's result, add back to the group's total profit.

When a subsidiary holds shares of its parent, Beams offers two treatments, the treasury stock approach and the conventional approach. PSAK 232 treats parent shares held by any group member as treasury shares, deducted from equity at cost, so the treasury stock approach is the one that fits Indonesian standards. Holdings between subsidiaries are eliminated, and there is no treasury alternative for them.
